speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure in informing the house that today there appears an announcement in the London Gazette that by virtue of letters patent Her Majesty the Queen has conferred upon His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh the style and dignity of a prince of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It is indicated in the announcement that it is Her Majesty's wish that henceforth His Royal Highness should be known as His Royal Highness the Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh. I know that all hon. members and the people of Canada will rejoice with us at this high recognition which Her Majesty has bestowed upon His Royal Plighness who, over recent years, has been tireless in his worldwide services on behalf of the crown and of the commonwealth.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext:
I should like to inform the house that the governor general has just approved the appointment of a royal commission to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland in accordance with section 29 of the terms of union with Newfoundland. The terms of reference of the commission are of course those set forth in that section of the terms of union.
We have been fortunate in securing the services as commissioners of Hon. John McNair, chief justice of New Brunswick, who will be the chairman, Hon. Sir Albert Walsh, chief justice of the supreme court of Newfoundland, and Professor John Deutsch of the University of British Columbia, a distinguished former public servant of Canada. I should like to lay on the table two copies of the order in council establishing the commission.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister when it is expected that commission will be able to commence its work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I assume it will commence its work almost immediately. It will no doubt, as other royal commissions have done, have a preliminary meeting to determine the procedure that the commissioners will follow in making their investigation and probably determining the time within which they will expect to receive briefs from the government of Newfoundland and those in Newfoundland who may wish to make representations. There will also no doubt be representations made on behalf of the government of Canada with the information we have about the facts that will have to be the basis of whatever recommendations the commission will find it opportune to make in strict accord with the terms of union which, as the hon. gentleman will remember, were confirmed by an act of this parliament and by an act of the parliament at New Westminster because it has a bearing upon the whole of the British North America Act and its amendments.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question? Will it be possible to include some of the general problems of the Atlantic region under this commission, even though it may be a little bit further than the terms of union?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; this commission will be restricted to carrying out the terms of union. They will probably have to examine what the position is in the Atlantic region in order to come to a conclusion with respect to the maintenance of public services in Newfoundland equal to those that prevail in the Atlantic area without a heavier burden of provincial taxation in Newfoundland than in the other provinces of the Atlantic area. Those will be matters that they will have to look into. But from the qualifications of the members of the commission I expect and hope that their recommendations will be strictly in accord with the terms of union that were sanctioned by parliament at the time the union took place.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext:
I should like to address a question to the Prime Minister with reference to the announcement which was just made regarding the royal commission. Is the Prime Minister of the opinion that the terms of reference will be sufficiently broad to allow an inquiry

Inquiries of the Ministry into the working conditions and job opportunities of employees of Canadian National Railways who, I understand, have been affected under this one section?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS NEWFOUNDLAND  APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON REVISION OF TERMS OF UNION
speechtext: I think the hon. lady is quite as competent as I could be to interpret the terms of union and the manner in which such distinguished jurists as the chief justice of New Brunswick and the chief justice of Newfoundland, and such a competent economist as Mr. John Deutsch, will feel it their duty to interpret them in order to carry out the intent of that clause of the terms of union.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister bring the house up to date with regard to the situation in the Suez canal. We read dispatches to the effect that Egypt is now delaying the clearing of the canal. Yesterday afternoon there were press dispatches to the effect that she had rejected the proposal of Great Britain, the United States and Norway for the temporary operation of the canal once it is cleared. Canada has quite a large stake in this clearance of the canal. I was wondering whether the Prime Minister could tell us what the actual situation is at the present time?

subtopic: SUEZ CANAL'
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. I have no official information that goes beyond what has been reported in the newspapers. I have seen over the last few days these reports that there was delay in the operations but there has been no report yet to that effect from General Wheeler who is in charge of the operations.
With respect to the proposals that had been made as to the manner in which the canal would be operated after it was cleared, those proposals were made by the principal users of the canal of which, as the hon. gentleman knows, Canada is not one; and we have no official information in that regard. As the hon. gentleman knows, there is still uncertainty as to whether the debate is going to take place this morning or whether there is to be another postponement. Our information was that the debate would begin this morning, when the attitude to be taken by the various members will become officially known.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGALITY OF MARRIAGE CEREMONIES AT SIX NATIONS RESERVATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Since he has advised us that he is a good boy scout and since good boy scouts generally admit mistakes I wonder whether he is still not satisfied that the Ontario government considers legal all marriages performed previously to July 1, 1956, by an Indian chief in the traditional Long House ceremony?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGALITY OF MARRIAGE CEREMONIES AT SIX NATIONS RESERVATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting for days for the hon. gentleman to ask this question so I could admit that my pipe line to Queen's Park is evidently not quite as good as his.
In view of the great interest there seems to be in this question of Long House marriages I perhaps might be permitted to make a brief statement about it. Those marriages which are performed on the Six Nations Indian reserve according to the Long House rites have, as a matter of fact, recently been recognized by the government of Ontario. I received a report from the director of Indian affairs on this subject about 10 minutes after I left the house after the hon. gentleman asked his question the other day and it was to the effect that the government of Ontario has now decided, regardless of whether they are registered or not, to recognize all marriages performed according to Long House rites before July 1,	1956, as legitimate
marriages. As a consequence, the registrar of the Indian affairs branch of my department is proceeding immediately to make the necessary corrections in the band lists. There are a number of other cases affected as well as the one the hon. gentleman was asking about.
Since the action taken by the Ontario government was taken at the request of my department and as a result of a conference I had with the council of the band during a visit to the reserve on September 27, 1955, 82715-99
Inquiries of the Ministry I should like to express warm appreciation of this co-operation from the Ontario authorities.
The recognition of marriages performed before July 1, 1956, will assist the Indian affairs branch of my department in dealing with a number of outstanding problems. Unfortunately, the whole problem is not yet satisfactorily solved.
My understanding is that the legislation of the Ontario legislature provides for the licensing of chiefs of the Long House to perform marriages and for the registration of such marriages by the chiefs. Up to the present some of the chiefs, not all of them, have not been willing to comply with the provision regarding licensing and registration though others have done so. I sincerely hope that the whole matter will be satisfactorily worked out in the very near future so that unfortunate situations such as that which prompted the questions in the house recently will not recur.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGALITY OF MARRIAGE CEREMONIES AT SIX NATIONS RESERVATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. Is the minister willing to admit that it is his responsibility to have the Long House chieftains register themselves with the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: STATEMENT ON LEGALITY OF MARRIAGE CEREMONIES AT SIX NATIONS RESERVATION

Well, sir, this is a free
country and if these free citizens of Canada do not choose to act in a certain way, in their relations with the provincial authorities, I know of no law of this parliament or any other power inherent in me to compel them to do so and I hope there never will be such a law.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. W, E. Harris (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 158, to amend the Municipal Grants Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the debate on the resolution a great many questions were asked and a number of opinions expressed concerning the contents of this bill. The bill has only been distributed overnight and I am sure that hon. members have had an opportunity to see it but have not had sufficient time to consider it at great length.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Municipal Grants Act
However, last night I announced that it would be our intention this year to do what we did on former occasions, that is, have the bill go to the standing committee on banking and commerce. I could at this time answer questions directed to me but it seems that if I answered the questions the answers would probably not be the kind of answers which hon. gentlemen might have expected because of my inability to project myself fully into their minds. That might lead to further questions and debate.
I would suggest to the house that since all members who spoke agreed with the principle of the bill and the only questions were with respect to the interpretation of the clauses in it, and that in general they thought we ought to be going a lot further in solving what was considered to be the municipal problem my suggestion is that we do not protract the second reading debate but rather that we wait until the bill reaches the standing committee on banking and commerce where specific questions with respect to airports and buildings of one kind or another in the respective constituencies could be answered better.
May I then just answer the general complaint with respect to the bill which was made by a good many hon. members who spoke. They quoted what I had said in introducing the resolution to the effect that this was not a solution of the municipal problem. They made reference particularly to the fact that action being taken had nothing to do with the fiscal need of the municipal corporations and on that based their objections that since that seemed to be the motive behind the bill there ought to be another motive, namely, the solution of the problem of municipal corporations, their taxation rights and the like.
I only wish to add that my remarks were apropos and I think correct in that there is nothing in the bill except with respect to the payment of grants in lieu of taxes to municipal corporations. I do not profess in the bill to be dealing in any manner whatever with the problems municipal corporations may have. The intention is solely that of providing for the payment of a grant in lieu of taxes to municipal corporations where there is federal property. I agree that there are details with which hon. members might disagree, but on the larger issue of whether or not municipal corporations should have the opportunity of a dominion-provincial-municipal conference to allocate further fields of taxation, whether or not the share of the tax dollar so called, which I think has been referred to by every opposition speaker, is

correct or whether or not a different interpretation could be applied, that does not seem to me germane to the particular debate at the moment.
Let me point out, however, that those who quoted the Gordon report with respect to the problems of the municipalities might with equal advantage, I think, have gone on to quote the rest of their remarks in which mention was made that the income of the municipal corporations with respect to personal disposable income is lower at the present time than it has ever been before. I would not want to add anything more to that although those who read the report will see what conclusion the royal commission came to with respect to that particular fact.
I do want to add, however, that so far as we have been able to do so in drafting the bill it is not the intention to withdraw from any position we have taken up to the present time and that the results should be increased payments of grants in any of the circumstances under which grants are now being made and in addition, of course, other municipal corporations will obtain a grant where they have not already done so.
I do think, however, that the specific details would be dealt with better in the standing committee which has the matter fresh in its mind because it considered the amendment of only two years ago. Therefoie, sir, I would prefer to answer questions there at some length and if they are not fully answered to the satisfaction of hon. members there will, of course, be a further debate when the bill comes back to committee of the whole.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister is justified in having said that the principle of the bill has met with approval. I also appreciate the force of his suggestion that questions might perhaps be more conveniently answered before the banking and commerce committee. I regret, as a matter of fact, that we did not press him to answer further questions when we were at the resolution stage but that is over now. I do not propose to debate the matter further at the present time.
The minister has been very frank in pointing out the limitations of the bill and actually the bill deals almost wholly with the details of the application of the extension which is brought about. The minister referred in particular to one aspect of the Gordon report with regard to the percentage of disposable income. I would simply remind the minister that it is small comfort to people who find their municipal taxes perhaps a trifle lower percentagewise because after all it is they who

are paying the terrifically high taxes to the federal level of government.
While we recognize, as the minister has pointed out, the definite limitations of this particular bill, I hope when we go to the banking and commerce committee there will be recognition of the fact pointed out so generally throughout the debate that the legislation does not make a dint at all in the larger problem and that we shall be able to pursue that argument further and perhaps make progress in the minister's mind at least in convincing him and through him his colleagues that this problem, which as so many of us tried to emphasize in the debate is a pressing one, is crying out for treatment and that we are not acting our age if we rely wholly on this present very small instalment of what needs to be done.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED CAPITAL OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take any more time to discuss this resolution. However last evening the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance saw fit to refer to some remarks I had made previously, and I propose to deal briefly with the matter at the present time. A week ago, Mr. Chairman, I had this to say concerning the farm loan board, as recorded at page 1326 of Hansard:
About the only thing we gained from that lengthy discussion was an improvement in the application form that is used in applying for loans.
I wish to point out that I said about the only thing we gained from last year's work on this particular topic was an improvement in the application form that was used by the Canadian farm loan board. I meant that, Mr. Chairman. However, last night the parliamentary assistant had this to say about the matter. I should like to quote from page 1535 of Hansard:
One hon. member, I believe it was the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose, suggested that out of that labour of last session, including the work of the banking and commerce committee he felt little had developed except we had streamlined the application form. I feel that is an uninformed statement, Mr. Chairman, to say the least.
Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary assistant is entitled to his own opinion. On the other hand I should like him to respect my right to an opinion as well.

Canadian Farm Loan Act
I have in my hand the report of the Canadian farm loan board for the year ended March 31, 1956. Dealing with the activities of the Canadian farm loan board in the four western provinces I find that in 1955 the number of first mortgage loans that were granted in British Columbia was 100 and that last year it was 94. In the province of Alberta, in 1955 307 first mortgage loans were granted; in 1956 there were 314 such loans granted. In Saskatchewan in 1955 726 first mortgage loans were granted and in 1956 there were 671. In Manitoba in 1955 200 first mortgage loans were granted and in 1956 there were 229.
I know the parliamentary assistant is extremely anxious to impress upon the members of the committee the fact that there has been an improvement. We are prepared to admit that there has been an improvement in the Canadian Farm Loan Act over the years, from $5,000 maximum to $10,000 maximum to $15,000 maximum. We are ready to concede that fact, Mr. Chairman. But we also remember the days of the change from the oxcart to the horse to the T-model Ford. As far as I am personally concerned the activities of the farm loan board are just about as modern as is the T-model Ford.
In comparing the years 1955 and 1956 as to the numbers of first mortgage loans, I find that the number in 1956 was down by 25 as compared with what it was in 1955 in the four western provinces.
Coming to loans granted on second mortgage, I find that in the province of British Columbia in 1955 there were four such loans granted and in 1956 there were four such loans granted. In Alberta in 1955 there were 33 such loans granted and in 1956 there were 16 such loans granted. In Saskatchewan in 1955 there were 237 loans granted under second mortgage and last year only 124. In the province of Manitoba in 1955 there were 51 loans granted under second mortgage and only 13 in 1956. In other words, comparing the two years 1955 and 1956, I find that there was a decrease of 168 loans in 1956 as compared with the number granted in 1955.
Mr. Chairman, in my language that is not progress. It just means that the farmers of those four western provinces are not able to make the use of this farm loan board that they should be able to make. It is true that, comparing those two years, the total amount lent to the farmers of those provinces increased last year slightly over $13,000 above the figure in 1955. But we must remember, Mr. Chairman, that $13,000 is not the maximum of one loan which could be granted under the act as it stands at the present time.

Last Friday I put on the record five recommendations which this group would make to the parliamentary assistant and, through him, to the Minister of Finance as to things which we feel should be done immediately in order to make the farm loan board operative in such a fashion that it will be of use to the farmers of Canada. At that time I suggested that the maximum loan granted be increased from $15,000 to $20,000. Second, I suggested that the term of repayment of the loan be extended from 30 years to 40 years and that the amount of the loan which is granted upon the appraised valuation be extended from 65 per cent as it is at the present time to 80 per cent. I also suggested at that time that a good look should be taken at the possibility of lowering the interest rate charged on loans under the farm loan act. Finally, Mr. Chairman, I said that I felt that a more optimistic or realistic approach should be made to the whole matter of appraisal of farm property in order to bring it in line with present-day valuations of farm property and the cost of machinery and equipment that go to make up the farm.
I do not feel that I am alone in this matter, Mr. Chairman. I know that the farm organizations of western Canada or of Canada as a whole are greatly concerned about the activities of the Canadian farm loan board. Just this week the Interprovincial Farm Union Council presented a brief to the government and in it they had this to say-I am quoting from page 3. This deals with credit and so on:
Fifty per cent of the farms in Canada are undercapitalized and as a result receive low or subsistence incomes. The solution of the problem facing these units lies in increasing either their actual size or their total production. Either course will require increased capital. This capital will have to be provided in the form of long-term and intermediate credit at low interest rates. The credit advanced should be directed to the farmers who need it. That is, particularly to those in the low-income group or to younger farmers who are commencing farm operations.
Just there, Mr. Chairman, I wish to point out to you that we must do something to encourage young men to get back to the farm. In the last few years the trend has been for them to leave the farm. Within a few years we are going to find our farms in Canada manned by a group of tired old men if something is not done soon. To continue the quotation from the brief:
It should be available for expansion in land or buildings and for purchase of livestock and equipment necessary to put the unit on an economic basis.
Farther on in the brief we find this:
In view of the displacement that has been and still is taking place on our farms, . . .

That is the continual change with respect to people living on our farms.
-we cannot emphasize too strongly the need for implementation of this credit policy, so that the present crop of potential farmers may not be lost to the industry.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is a serious situation which is worthy of great concern on the part of the government. Then again the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its brief which was submitted to the members of the cabinet on February 15 dealt with this matter. Under the title of "Farm Credit" they had this to say:
A great many farmers, indeed, put improvement in present farm credit policies at the top of the list of those matters which require action by the federal government.
I want to emphasize that quotation.
This organization is speaking for the farmers of Canada just as the interprovincial farm union speaks for a large section of the farmers of Canada. I continue quoting:
There is, first of all, the matter of the Canadian Farm Loan Board Act. Some improvements in this act were made at the last session-
I submit that I am conscious of the improvements that were made last year and, small though they were, they were improvements.
-of parliament, particularly in respect to the maximum size of the loan-
Yes, that is true.
-the length of term of mortgages and the percentage of the appraised value which may be loaned. We feel, however, that much more needs to be done to put the operation of the Canadian Farm Loan Board on a satisfactory basis. The unanimous opinion of those of our members who have had occasion to deal with the board is that its appraisal and lending policy is unnecessarily cautious and conservative. The result is that the young man who looks to the board as a source of credit for getting established in farming finds that the amount which is available from the board is entirely inadequate to his purposes. We would recommend a review and liberalization of the board's appraisal practices, and legislative provision for increasing the percentage of the appraised value that may be borrowed by farmers, especially where the amount of money borrowed is moderate.
I do feel that in speaking last Friday perhaps I made a mistake. But it is not the type of mistake that the parliamentary assistant says I made. I said that about the only thing that was gained as a result of last year's discussion of the matter was an improvement in the application form. Perhaps I should have said that was the only thing that mattered to the farmers of the west; that is about all they gained from it. The story this year is that the number of loans granted as compared with last year is down; the amount of money, on the other hand, is up.

While I am on my feet the hon. member for Assiniboia and I had a discussion last night which appears at page 1540 of yesterday's Hansard, and I promised to recheck certain information that was sent to me by an assistant at my request while I was sitting in my seat. This information referred to a comparison of the percentage of loans that are given by the central mortgage and housing corporation as compared with loans from the farm loan board. I confess that my figures were in the wrong order. The 90 per cent of the loan applies to the first portion of the loan and the 70 per cent to the latter portion of the loan. been insured, and in addition to that the rate of interest is more favourable under the farm loan board. Then, of course, the maximum amount of loan is greater under the farm loan board act.

speechtext:
There is just one point that I should like the parliamentary assistant to clear up and that is the definition under agricultural production value. The hon. member who spoke a moment ago spoke of the valuation of the farm.
We have rather a peculiar situation in the maritime provinces. Many of our farms have what is known as a wood lot or a lumber lot. Perhaps this matter has been brought to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. The lumber lot is considered by the farmer to be perhaps one of the most important assets of his farm. My understanding is that, under the interpretation of the agricultural productive value, that wood lot is not taken into consideration as far as the land is concerned. The result is that many farmers do feel that they are entitled to a loan because they have the value in the farm in- the form of their wood lot, their land under cultivation and their buildings, but yet they are being turned down. Can that interpretation be relaxed so as to give more consideration to these farmers?
In the Gordon report this matter of farms in New Brunswick and in other parts of eastern Canada has been considered very carefully. According to the report there are in New Brunswick many farms which rely to a great extent on this lumber land. I may say that the lumber on this land is not all stripped or cut in one year. Many of the farmers are now cutting what they consider the annual growth in perhaps two or three years' time. It really is a productive crop on the farm.
The Gordon report also stated that there are many farms that should be allowed to grow up in lumber again. It is a very valuable asset and perhaps there are other lands such as marshlands in other sections which should be considered for more cultivation. This matter is to be investigated and studied, I believe, by a committee appointed in the Senate, headed by our good friend Senator Power. May I say my personal opinion is that they could not have chosen a better man than Senator Power to head this committee.
There is another point that was brought up the other day, and it has reference to the returned man not receiving as much consideration as perhaps he should. I know of many cases of returned men who, if they go out and work at some other job and have their farms looked after perhaps by hired men, or some of their families, are prejudiced in their applications for loans. Many of them

are having quite a difficult time and they find it necessary to supplement their incomes by doing other work. I would like to hear the parliamentary assistant comment on these two points, which I know are important and of concern to the people affected.
Mention was made of the number of applications from the different provinces. I know from the last report of the Canadian farm loan board that there were 25, I think, from my own province which is a very small number. If the regulations were relaxed I think we would find there would be more applications, and I feel that much more assistance could be given to the farmers in my area. They can give good security in the form of their lumber lots, and they certainly need the money.

If I may follow that up
with another question, Mr. Chairman, last evening and again today the parliamentary assistant mentioned the appointment of an appraiser as one of the examples of the liberalization of the act, or the procedure under the act. I am rather curious about that because I am wondering what effect this appointment may have. Does it mean that only one appraiser has been appointed to act as a sort of chief appraiser for the board in co-operation with the local appraisers? If so, what procedure has been evolved for the synchronization of values? On the face of it, I fail to see where the appointment of one appraiser for operations in nine provinces, or perhaps even 10 provinces, could have any material effect on synchronizing the approval of values unless there was something done to follow that up, unless the appraisers on the local level were called into regional conferences or schools, or some other agreed-upon method was laid out. I would like to get some clarification on that point from the hon. member.
While I am waiting for that I wish to mention this, too. I think it would be wise wherever possible to make greater use of

Canadian Farm Loan Act the assessors that are present in every rural municipality, I suppose across the country. Particularly in the prairie provinces, the assessors that are appointed by rural municipalities are usually men of fairly high qualification who know their jobs and who go out and make a detailed appraisal from farm to farm. They know the quality of the soil, the condition of the buildings and the general capacity of the land to produce and so forth in order to arrive at their assessment. All that data is available on the record and it should be put to use.
This could be done in two ways. One way I would suggest is that wherever possible a municipal assessor be appointed the local appraiser. I have found that for one reason or another that is not done in our part of the country at least and I have also found that appraisers have been appointed who have had no previous contact with that kind of work whereas many of the municipal assessors who are on a part time basis in my opinion would be excellent for the job. Secondly, during the winter months, as the parliamentary assistant would appreciate there is a hold-up in connection with applications owing to the fact that the land is covered with snow and road conditions are bad. It so happens that in many cases, in Manitoba at least, farmers who intend to apply for a loan make up their minds about it in the fall for reasons I do not need to enumerate. It is fairly obvious that the autumn is the time of year when they are usually more familiar with their financial position than they are at any other time. In most cases the farmers are asked to wait until spring to have an appraisal made. Since most of the necessary information with regard to individual farms has been compiled in the books of the assessor at the municipal office it would seem to me that in most cases all that the local appraiser would need to do would be to walk over to the assessor's office and sit down with him and examine the books. Although he could not make a physical appraisal he could obtain excellent information from the man who is most familiar with the individual farms. In my opinion this would go a long way toward avoiding the lengthy delays which are so irritating to the individual applicant whose plans in connection with the loan are held up for two or three months or even longer waiting until spring when the appraisal is made.
I hope the parliamentary assistant will give consideration to these matters because I think they are practical suggestions which will help the board to do the kind of job it is expected to do. The chief criticism as far as I am aware has been the long delays
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
and the fact that the farmer who applies in the fall at the time of year when he is endeavouring to make plans for his spring operations is frequently left until late in the spring waiting for a decision concerning the loan and often it arrives too late for his purposes so he simply drops his application.

Mr. Chairman I, too, am pleased that an appraiser has been obtained by the board. There was a great deal of resistance in the committee last year to any suggestion that the type of personnel acting as appraisers could be improved. As a matter of fact I remember that in reply to one question it was said the people who were doing the appraising at that time were considered by the board far better authorities than some of the excellent and competent men to whom some of us were referring in our discussion.
This particular measure is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Finance. It seems to me that if you are going to have an agricultural credit policy that works effectively, if you are going to have a Canadian farm loan board that truly meets the needs of agriculture, you are far more apt to have a successful operation if the jurisdiction were transferred to the Department of Agriculture. I really cannot understand why it is kept under the Department of Finance when the board deals exclusively with agriculture and when the objective of the program should be other than making a profit. Certainly the same criteria that are used in judging whether or not other aspects of the Department of Finance are successful are not appropriate when it comes to judging the success of the Canadian farm loan board.
I wish to express my agreement with most of the suggestions that were made by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose concerning what improvements could be made. These have already been placed on the record a number of times and they include increasing the maximum amount of the loans to

$20,000, increasing to 90 per cent the percentage of appraised value on which a loan can be made, an extension of the loan period from the current maximum of 30 years to a maximum of 40 years and a general liberalization of the attitude and policies of the board in dealing with applications.
Last evening the parliamentary assistant placed on the record a great deal of valuable information concerning the operations of the board so far this year. In this respect I agree with the parliamentary assistant rather than the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose because I believe that within a ten-month period the board has made a highly commendable improvement in its operations. Both the number of loans and the total value of the loans for all of Canada have increased by approximately 50 per cent. In view of the fact that the parliamentary assistant appears to have a great deal of information concerning the operations of the board so far this year I am wondering if he is now in a position to say whether or not the board is likely to make a profit on its operations during the current fiscal year that will end in about one month's time. In other words has the inevitable increase in the cost of doing business, salaries, rentals and travelling expenses and so forth been such that the normal profit of the board is likely to be decreased or is it likely there will be a substantial net profit on March 31?

Canadian Farm Loan Act the board has been provided with a capital of $3 million and that capital has never returned a dividend. If my hon. friend will look at the annual report for last year he will see set out the net profits for the years ending in 1956 and 1955 which indicate that the board has been just about breaking even. The profit for the year ended March 31, 1956 was $173,175 after paying income tax of $45,000. As I say, no dividend whatsoever has been returned on this capital of $3 million.
I do not know of any business institution that would operate as closely as that. Here is a board which has obligations of some $45 million and loans of some $43 million and yet it makes a profit of only $173,175. I do not think it can be asserted that this board has as one of its objectives the making of money, but parliament never expected that this board would be subsidized by the taxpayers.
When the board was set up in 1929 the intention was not to provide all the farm credit required in Canada. It was intended that it should be a competitive operation carrying out a recommendation by a royal commission which pointed regrettably to what up to that time had been the very high interest rates charged generally for farm mortgages. The commission reported that up to that time interest rates generally were between 7 per cent and 12 per cent. The new board set an interest rate of 6 per cent which provided competition and some of the private lending companies in turn reduced their rates.
In addition the board provides loans to farmers in all types of years. It has not particularly reduced its lending in times of poorer economic conditions as is sometimes the practice of financial institutions. However, it was not intended that all farm borrowings would come from one source. As a matter of fact, as was mentioned last night, several of the provinces have their own farm credit organizations. Despite what hon. members from Ontario said yesterday, there was never any reference to the parallel lending organization in that province. This junior farm loan board is a fine organization operated by that province for young farmers.

Mr. Chairman, the emphasis placed by the parliamentary assistant upon the requirement that the board conduct its operations, including the rate on loans that it charges, in such a way as to make certain there is no loss suggests to me the great danger there is that within a relatively short time the board may in fact be forced to raise its interest rates to applicants. The information given to the committee last year in connection with the board's operations in 1955 showed that the cost of operating amounted to 1.39 per cent of the money acquired. Last night the parliamentary assistant gave us the disturbing information that the cost of money to the board from the government had gone up to 4 per cent. If my memory serves me correctly, a year ago that cost was around 3J per cent to 3J per cent. If you add to the 4 per cent the cost of operation on the basis of the 1955 cost you arrive at a figure in excess of 5 per cent.
I realize that there are other factors to be considered, mainly that a great part of the money the board has used was obtained at different rates, probably in all instances at lower rates, but nevertheless the increasing cost of money to the board along with the policy of the government of allowing interest rates to go up will in my opinion endanger the operations of this board at 5 per cent. I believe that this is an exceedingly important matter. It was stressed repeatedly before the committee last year, namely that the cost of money to the board and to farm operators should be decreased. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture placed on the record a year ago figures suggesting the great advantages that would flow from an interest rate to farmers of 3J per cent.
No one should believe that the agricultural industry on the basis of historic records can afford to pay a 5 per cent interest rate. It seems to me that the whole trend of the government's tight money policy is to saddle on the people of this country who can ill afford to pay it a burdensome and discriminatory interest charge. I notice that another resolution is to be introduced to provide loans to certain producers on the security of grain. Previously this legislation contained provision for a statutory rate of 5 per cent, but apparently now the rate is to be left wide open at the discretion of the governor in

council. That suggests just one thing to me, that the government is paving the way for a further hike in interest rates to producers by these measures.
I believe the country should know at this time what is the intention of the government with respect to interest rates to be charged by this board. I submit we should be given some assurance that at least within the next twelve-month period the rate now charged by the board will be held. Last night the parliamentary assistant said he did not have his crystal ball with him, but I think the public are entitled to know whether or not this rate will be held for a further twelvemonth period. I think the parliamentary assistant should give the committee further information as to how the recent increases in the cost of money to the board are affecting the board's over-all costs. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant specifically to what extent the new 4 per cent rate has increased the over-all cost of money to the board and to what extent such a rate is reducing the potential profit of the board.

On the other hand, the farmer has not shared in the general increase in wealth production. If the hon. member will study the history of agriculture in Canada he will find that over the years the total net return on investment in farm lands and property has been 2 per cent. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED CAPITAL OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not participated in this discussion thus far because I felt it was being carried on very ably by the other members of our group who are members of our committee on agriculture, namely the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose.
I am quite proud of their accomplishment.
But I now feel that it would be in order to make one or two observations. In the first place, I do not grant that money lent for house building should be at a rate of 5 Jr per cent. I think it is practically a monstrosity that an interest rate of 5J per cent should be charged for money going into any productive enterprise in Canada at the present time.

Canadian Farm Loan Act
One of the main things which it seems the minister and the parliamentary assistant, who perhaps is bound hand and foot, overlook is the fact that money can be created in Canada today and is created by the Bank of Canada. It is not capital in the sense that money was capital 50 years ago when all the money that was available for use was money which had been earned by people and taken from them by taxation. Can we not by any conceivable means get it into the mentalities of the members of this house that the fact that the parliament of Canada through the Bank of Canada can create money without cost should enter into our whole attitude to all these questions?
In respect of the advance in the interest rate on money made available by the government to the farm loan board, I say it is simply an outrage that the government should increase the rate of interst the farm loan board has to pay on the money it uses, when you consider that that money could be made available by the Bank of Canada at not more than 2J per cent.
Even Bruce Hutchison knows today that our money can be created. In an article in Maclean's magazine of March 2 he shows a considerable amount of intelligence and enlightenment on that matter. Surely that knowledge should be able to get to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.
What I have said about the creation of money has a bearing on a great many things, but my particular object in rising to speak today is to comment on the need for large loans from this Canadian farm loan board and for loans for very long terms such as 40 years or the like at a low interest rate. All other of those matters no doubt were dealt with by both the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose but it will do no harm to repeat this important comment.
Why is it at the present time so important that farm loans should be long term, very large and at low rates of interest? There are several things which we, as members of parliament, are likely to fail to take cognizance of. The first one of those things is that in order to compete successfully today a farmer must have high-class machinery, and in grain farming high-class machinery is excessively costly. There are a great many different kinds of machines which the farmer must have every year. Much of that machinery is not in use any more than probably two months a year or even less. Consequently there is a heavy overhead on this machinery. At the present time under competitive conditions the farmer is helpless
[Mr. Blackmore.l
to do anything about the matter. He simply must have the machinery or he cannot possibly compete.
This is a condition which has arisen among us within the last 40 years; those of us who have derived our monetary ideas from those who lived 50 years ago are likely to be completely outdated.
Because of the great number of machines which are necessary today, the farmer is forced on a cash basis much more than ever before. In the days when men turned their horses, their then source of power, out to grass on the pastures and turned the grass into the equivalent of gasoline to run the machines, the situation was far different from that which obtains today when the farmer must pay hard money for every gallon of gasoline which he must have for every bit of travelling that he does and with which to do every bit of work he does on the farm with every machine that he runs. This puts our farmer in a condition unique in history, Mr. Chairman. Never in all the annals of mankind has a condition of that sort previously prevailed.
There is another aspect of this question also. Even when I was a small boy, if a machine broke down we were generally sufficiently skilled in mechanics to mend the ordinary machine we used such as a disc harrow, an ordinary harrow, a walking plow, double trees, chains and all that sort of thing. But let anything happen to any part of a machine which the farmer is running today, and what is the situation? Can he repair it? Even if he is a most skilful mechanic and is equipped with the finest kind of machinery, in most cases he is unable to repair that machine. That means that he has dollars to lay out immediately. Once more he is on a cash basis.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED CAPITAL OF BOARD
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED CAPITAL OF BOARD
speechtext:
Not for a little while. Another aspect of the question is that in order to make this expensive machinery pay, such as a $5,000 tractor, a farmer must have large holdings. On several occasions already it has been brought to the attention of the house that he must have at least a section of ground in heavy land and perhaps two sections of ground in light land. Land costs money and a great deal of it. On that amount of land the taxes are heavy, and the taxes are demanded of the farmer. Once more he is on a cash basis and he must have large amounts of money in order to negotiate as regards that land.
Because of the heavy capital investment the farmer has and because of the peculiar conditions which face him, he must have an opportunity to sell his product immediately

and get cash for it. There is no need of burdening any hon. member in this committee by repeating the difficulties our wheat farmers are experiencing by reason of the fact that they are unable to sell their grain immediately and get cash for it so that they can go out and pay their bills. Some may ask what connection that matter has with the points that I am discussing. It has a good deal of effect on the general situation.
Another aspect is the fact that it is extremely difficult for a man now running a farm of one section or of two sections to have a herd of hogs and feed them, a number of cows and milk them or a flock of chickens and take care of them. In other words, it is almost impossible for him to go into mixed farming which used to be the secret of subsistence farming from 60 years ago back. But today he is unable to put his eggs in more than about one basket. That fact again has an important bearing on this matter that we are discussing.
There is another important matter which is facing farming people everywhere. Men who have devoted their lives to the building up of a farm holding, when they reach the age of 70 years or probably 65 years, find that they have faced the weather and have put up with the roughness of life as long as they are able to do so. Hence they need to be able to turn their holdings over to the boy and the boy must have money. The father needs to be able to sell the land in his holding for probably $40,000 or $50,000, perhaps in order to discharge other obligations which he has. How is he going to be able to sell that land to his son? How is the son going to be able to take over the land unless there are available, facilities by means of which this boy can obtain the money which is necessary to pay his father and to put himself in a position to carry on and his father in a position to retire? This again demands large loans at small rates of interest over long periods of time. Why a long period of time? Because if you take into consideration the operations of the average farmer over a number of years, you will find that his losses in one year will have been such that it will take him four or five years to recoup them Over a long period of say 20 years, 30 years or 40 years, he is exceedingly fortunate if he keeps his head above water at all on a farm.
I speak as one who was born on a farm and raised on a farm and has been watching farming operations going on for all the years of his life. This is another matter which has a bearing.
I notice that the parliamentary assistant every once in a while talks about the cost of capital and that he acts as though there is
Canadian Farm Loan Act no other way whereby he can get money except by taking it out of the money market or taking it out of the taxes or the revenue fund of the country. His attitude there is absolutely fallacious and I will challenge him to prove in what respect it is not.
Now, if he wants to have others participating in the provision of the agricultural loans, like mortgage companies and so on, that is one matter; but we are not running our farm economy in order to give business to the mortgage companies. If we are, then we are running our economy straight into ruin ultimately. If we cannot begin to think in terms of obtaining money from the Bank of Canada at not more than 2.5 per cent interest, money which does not necessarily have to be paid back to the Bank of Canada within 15 or 20 years: if we cannot start thinking in terms of a monetary situation based on that state of affairs, then we are utterly inadequate in our generation to do the kind of thinking which needs to be done in dealing with the problems of our farmers in relation to the farm loan board.

speechtext:
I just want to i*iake a few brief remarks, Mr. Chairman. I was pleased when the parliamentary assistant pointed out that one of the greatest advantages of this legislation has been the fact that it has, in the past at least, tended to keep interest rates within reason. I know of some cases in my province where farmers have taken out mortgages and paid perhaps 7 per cent interest for more than 25 years, yet still had the total principal outstanding. If they had been in a position to borrow the money through the Canadian farm loan board at the rate of interest then prevailing they would have been able to pay off both the interest and the principal over that period by having an annual charge only one-tenth of 1 per cent greater than the 7 per cent. In that way, this legislation would serve a very useful purpose.
There is one thing that I suspect, although I could not find figures to prove it, and that is that applications for loans from the farm loan board increase when farm net income is low. In other words, I suspect the farmers are resorting to this as a means of tiding them over tough financial conditions. Perhaps the board is serving a useful purpose in that respect, but I should like to think of the agriculture industry being in a position where farmers had sufficient confidence they would borrow money from the loan board to increase their holdings, modernize their equipment, improve their buildings and that sort of thing. I am afraid that is true only in a relatively small percentage of cases.

Canadian Farm Loan Act
This legislation has been used to a great extent in my province, and I think the people administering it are to be congratulated on the work they have done. However, there is one difficulty so far as farmers are concerned, and that is the time lapse which occurs on some occasions in having their holdings appraised after making application for a loan. I was wondering if it would be possible to expedite the appraisal of land by employing more part-time appraisers. It is essential, of course, that interest rates be kept low, at least as low as they are at the present time. The federation of agriculture feels that they are already too high and, as has been pointed out, there has been some indication they might go higher. This would be unfortunate indeed.
In a statement to the federal-provincial agriculture conference in Ottawa in December 1956, the federation of agriculture had this to say. I know the parliamentary assistant is familiar with this, but I think it bears repetition.
Though both the Canadian Farm Loan Board Act and Farm Improvement Loan Act were amended at the last sess*m of parliament considerable further improvement is possible. The Canadian farm loan board in particular is not providing a satisfactory answer to the long-term credit problems of the Canadian farmer. Interest rates should be lower, the loan limits on appraised value should be raised and appraisals should be less conservative. In addition, there should be a first-class supervisory service available to farmers who obtain these loans, particularly loans up to $10,000.
Those are sentiments with which I agree because agriculture, unlike almost any other industry in this country, is not sharing in the prosperity of the country and is not receiving inflated prices for farm products. Farmers are paying inflated prices for what they have to buy and therefore the farmer is caught in a cost-price squeeze. I should like to reiterate the importance of keeping interest charges low if farmers are going to be able to carry on at all and obtain the sort of capital necessary to run a farm today.
I have a question I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant. I notice that in the annual report there are no figures given for Newfoundland. Of course, I know there is no local office in Newfoundland, but I believe that, theoretically at least, the board does business in Newfoundland. I should like to know what the position is with regard to that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, February 8, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Lesage-Mr. Robinson (Sim-coe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources Act to provide for the establishment of two national museums in lieu of one, as at the present time, to be known as the Canadian museum of natural history and the Canadian museum of human history.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the few
moments I had before five o'clock on February 8 when this resolution was introduced I stated that I approved of the proposal embodied in this resolution and that the division of the national museum into two separate branches, a museum of natural history and a museum of human history, would in my opinion facilitate desirable expansion and development in each branch. I did not intend to suggest by that, of course, that we should aim at rivalling forthwith the British museum, shall I say; but certainly the growth and expansion of our national museum should keep pace with the rapid growth and development of our country. In my opinion the present measure represents a useful means towards this end and the possibilities are as yet hardly touched upon.
On the various occasions on which I have visited the national museum in Ottawa I have always taken a great deal of interest in the different exhibits. However, I am always particularly glad to note that in addition to exhibits of various minerals, some of which come from the Minas basin shore of my constituency, there is one exhibit there to which my own constituency can lay exclusive claim. That is the exhibit of petrified tree trunks and the other things which come from the Joggins area in my constituency. I dare say the Joggins exhibit is familiar to a good many hon. members of this house. I might point out that the Joggins area is one of the most interesting to geologists that can be found anywhere.
I think that an exhibit like this-and this is something to which I shall refer in a moment-may serve an extremely useful purpose here in Ottawa, where so many people from central Canada are in a position to enjoy the museum, in stimulating their interest in the particular area or region of the country from which the particular exhibit comes.
Concerning the field of human history in the present museum I always find the exhibits of the aboriginal inhabitants of this
country most interesting. Coming again to my own part of the country, I think it is well known that Nova Scotia presents one of the most fascinating stories of any province in Canada in the realm of human history. I think we all know that this applies to what we might call recorded or post-Columbian history and it also applies to unrecorded or pre-Columbian history.
There is a wealth of history concerning the natives who inhabited this country long before Columbus came to America. It is well known of course that a couple of centuries ago when England and France were struggling for the mastery of this continent the isthmus of Chignecto, which connects Nova Scotia with New Brunswick, was one of the most strategic points in the whole struggle.
In fact for many years it was known as the key to the continent. I may be out of order in saying this, but I suggest that the building of this canal across this isthmus would go a long way to solve many of the economic problems of the maritimes.
Long before Columbus the occupiers of what is now known as Nova Scotia were a tribe of Indians known as the Micmacs. I have often thought it most unfortunate that the present museum does not contain any individual record of those Indians. It may be that as they were part of the great Algonquin stock which occupied a great part of North America, and as there are Algonquin exhibits in the museum, this was not thought necessary but the fact is that the Micmacs possessed many unique customs and traditions. I submit that a record of their ways deserves a prominent place in our Canadian museum of human history.
When a separate museum of human history is set up in accordance with the principle of this resolution I do hope that the great Mic-mac tribe will have a place set aside in it in which to exhibit evidence of their ways and customs and beliefs. I am told for example that their tongue was among the most musical of all Indian languages, and in addition their religious beliefs and mythology were well advanced.
In this connection what is of particular interest to me is the legend of their semideity Glooscap. The centre of his activities and exploits was in Minas basin, which is an important part of my constituency, including the town of Parrsboro. I think it might be of interest to some hon. members, and certainly it will be of interest to the Minister of Fisheries whom I see in his seat, to know that Glooscap has recently been linked or an attempt has been made to link him with preColumbian European explorers.
It is generally regarded as an historical fact that the Norsemen coasted the shores of Nova
1572	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Northern Affairs and National Resources Scotia a thousand years ago, but an eminent United States writer, by the name of Frederick Pohl, who has interested himself in this subject, asserts that an Earl of Orkney, who bore the great name of Sinclair-probably he was an ancestor of our Minister of Fisheries- crossed the Atlantic with a considerable fleet and a considerable number of retainers in the year 1398, nearly a century before Columbus sailed. He reached the shores of Nova Scotia and spent the winter on the shores of Minas basin, then sailed back home leaving behind a tradition of a God-like white man. I think the descendant of that man shows some of the same traits. In the intervening decades that fact was developed by the Micmacs into their legend of Glooscap. I am not saying that I accept that as a truth, but at least it is interesting.
I mention these things simply to show the interest there is in the history of the Micmac tribe. I believe their history, their customs and their beliefs should be given a prominent place in the proposed museum of human history. We might regard that as simply a tribute to a wronged and ruined race, but then it perhaps could be considered on a more practical ground. This same principle could be expanded in many other directions. I suggest that such an exhibit here in Ottawa would tend to greatly increase tourist interest in the region from which these Indians came, the region of their ancestral home.
As I say, this idea could be expanded into many other regions of the country. For that reason I would recommend that this matter be studied and in this new museum of human history particular attention be given to the Indians who years ago occupied the peninsula of Nova Scotia. We know that pictures from the national gallery are sometimes sent on tour around the country so that people in other sections may have an opportunity to see them. It occurs to me that it might be feasible to have certain exhibits from the national museum taken on tour to those areas of the country where they are of local interest.
For instance, if an exhibit of Micmac work were exhibited in the town of Parrsboro in my constituency I know there would be a tremendous number of people in that area who would visit it. Living in the area where the Micmacs flourished they would be particularly interested in that sort of thing. I think it would prove a valuable stimulus to the tourist trade in addition to the other attractions which the region presents of unrivalled beauty of sea and shore, the highest tides in the world, the most picturesque golf course in the world located at Parrsboro.
[Mr. Lusby.)

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when the resolution was last under discussion I made a few brief remarks. I have several comments I should like to make and suggestions I should like to offer resulting from those visits. First I should like to know what are the plans of the government in the development of this museum of human history and museum of natural history. It is apparent that if all aspects of human history which are available for discovery are put under one roof it will require a building as large as the Victoria museum, if not larger. Could the minister give some information as to whether he plans to incorporate some of the archives in the museum of human history? The war museum is related to human history although in a slightly different sense.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: No definite decision has been made? Is it the intention to move the national gallery from the Victoria museum and to use that museum exclusively for the museum of natural history and erect a separate building for the museum of human history?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: It is expected that within two years the geological surveys branch and the national gallery will have left the Victoria museum. For some time the two museums will be housed in the same building, but planning is under way for a second building to house one of the museums. That is in the future. When the geological surveys branch and the national gallery leave the Victoria museum we will have an increase of two-thirds in the space and for some time after that it will be sufficient to house both museums. But the long-range planning is to have a separate building for each museum.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
I am very pleased to hear that because I am certainly one of those who advocate that the maximum possible advantage be taken of research into what has taken place in the past and displaying the results of such research to the public.
That brings up another question, the function of the whole national museum. It is apparent to me that much of the time of the staff is involved in research, the discovery of historic sites and the interpretation of the evidence discovered. At the same time the museum has also served as a place to display such discoveries publicly. It seems to me

Northern Affairs and National Resources
there are two conflicting objectives because if you study projects and devote two-thirds of your staff and space to that work you will automatically limit the opportunity of displays for the benefit of the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: Most of the studies are made outside the museum. They are made in the field so they do not take any space. As the hon. member knows, the space available in the present museum is very small and it has been impossible to do justice to the exhibits we have. We have been rotating them as much as we can but not to the extent that would provide a good showing of all the exhibits we have stored around Ottawa waiting for space in which they can be exhibited. As a matter of fact, I am in the process now of obtaining from my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, some space in another building near the museum in order to try to start the work immediately on the exhibits that we will be able to show in 1959 when we have the space available.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: I am right in assuming from what the minister has said that the primary purpose of the museum is for public display.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: The primary purpose of the museum is for public education through display and through publications, but in order to do that there must be some research done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: I can appreciate what the minister is saying but I am inclined to disagree with him because if you send out an anthropological field expedition to work in some diggings in an effort to determine the past history of civilization in Canada the result will be that chips of teeth, pieces of bone and beads will be found which are of no significance at all for public display purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: Oh yes, they can be displayed in such a way with such explanations that they will have significance not only for the people who see them but for our national entity, I would say.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
1 agree, but the minister has answered my question a little too soon. Before these things can be put on public display many hours of work must go into piecing them together and tying them into a larger pattern. It seems to me that a considerable amount of the time of the staff is spent on research and they must be skilled people in order to do the job, which brings up still another problem. Will the legislation recently passed by the house establishing the Canada Council permit scholarships and fellowships to be given to the technical staff working for the museum on research projects? I think that is quite an important point
because if university people are to receive scholarships or fellowships for anthropological or biological research then the pay schedules of these people will be higher than the present salary schedules of the museum staff. You will find that the museum will be a poor relation from the point of view of competing for technical staff to carry out these research functions. Since the museum certainly is associated with the culture of Canada, I am wondering whether the staff will qualify for grants from the Canada Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: The question had not entered my mind. It is there now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
I think it is rather important because right now we find that our salary schedules are such that we have United States citizens filling responsible positions on the museum staff. Perhaps we should not object to an American citizen holding a position but my view certainly is that an American citizen should not have the position if a Canadian citizen has the necessary qualifications. If our salary schedules are going to be low we will find ourselves in the position of having to use inferior and unqualified staff on this very important work.
My general comment on the museum is that it actually is a poor reflection of the capabalities of Canada. The minister has recognized that fact and I am appreciative that the government has finally seen fit to take this move to expand and develop the museum. At the same time I would point out to the minister and hon. members that if we are going to make an honest attempt to develop the museum, if we are going to have the finances necessary for the staff to go on research expeditions and to display properly the results of their investigations, we cannot be too parsimonious. In this year's estimates expenditures on the national museum amount to approximately $400,000, a pretty small amount compared with the tremendous job the museum is doing, particularly if we contrast the amount provided for the museum with the amounts provided for the national gallery of Canada and the design centre, both of which are in excess of $400,000.
I am not saying that the national gallery is getting too much. It is apparent, however, that the national museum is getting far too little. We will find ourselves in a position where we are going to have to deny trained archaeologists the opportunity to go out on field expedition because of lack of finances and we will certainly be missing an opportunity to explore some of Canada's past, which the minister agrees is so important. With respect to the move to build a truly national museum of which all
1574	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources Canadians can be proud I have a suggestion to make. As mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River on a previous occasion, there are a limited number of people who are able to visit the museum in Ottawa and if travelling exhibits can be made available it will do much to promote an interest in and an appreciation of our Canadian culture.
One method the government has followed is the use of travelling displays of Eskimo art. That has been done to such an extent that there is not a decent Eskimo art exhibit in the museum. They have all been sent overseas or sold with the result that we have not really got a display of Eskimo art to show the abilities of the people of that part of Canada, something that is generally unknown to most Canadians.
Finally, I wish the minister luck in his endeavour and I hope he will be able to impress upon his colleagues the need of providing adequate funds to secure qualified personnel to work for the museum in a research capacity and adequate funds to display in an attractive fashion the results of their findings so that they can be a part of the Canadian heritage.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question or two. When I was speaking the other day I referred to two aspects of this question, one being the size of staff that would be required in each of these museums in the capital city and the other being the possibility of giving financial assistance to some of our museums throughout the country. I mentioned particularly the outstanding display in the museum in Banff national park and the other at Drumheller. They are contributing a great deal to the culture of Canada. Is the minister prepared now to answer these questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
The additions to staff for the coming fiscal year will be as follows. There was one curator for the museum namely Dr. Alcock. He retired last fall. I wish to pay tribute to Dr. Alcock for the tremendous job he has been doing in all the years that he has been curator of the museum. With all the difficulties that have been mentioned by hon. members and by myself as to limitations with regard to space and the amount of money available, he has done an outstanding job as curator of the museum. Because we could foresee some possible expansion of the museum, and as had been recommended by the Massey commission, we decided to divide the museum into two branches pending the adoption of the legislation which is now before us, each with a director at its head. The director of the branch of natural history is Dr. L. S. Russell and the director of the branch of human


history is Dr. Jacques Rousseau, formerly of Montreal, who was director of the Montreal botanical garden. They are two outstanding men in their fields of endeavour. We had the chance of having those two gentlemen take over at the time that Dr. Alcock felt that he should retire.

They were created last fall and there is no increase over that, starting from the 1st of April: There is one administrative officer, one anthropologist, one clerk and two stenographers. speechtext:
When he starts talking like

Northern Affairs and National Resources reply. However, I place on his remarks the value which I think they merit, and that is not much. In Toronto there is the Royal Ontario Museum which I believe is the outstanding museum in Canada and one which is a great credit not only to Toronto but to the whole country. If I remember correctly, that museum could be considered as a museum both of natural history and of human history. It is a first-class modern museum and I have never heard of any suggestion that there should be two museums or that it would be much better if there were two instead of one.
The museum here in Ottawa does not begin to compare with the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto at the present time.
