maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the reason is that the Quebec museum, like the Royal Ontario museum, is dealing with only part of the country's natural history and human history, while the national museum has to deal with both on a national basis. The best evidence of that can be obtained from the people who know history and who know something about museums. I think the best evidence was given before the Massey commission when it sat. This commission not only recommended two museums, but recommended more than that. They recommended that the present museum be created a museum of natural history, and that there be created also museums of human history and science and that we should have zoological gardens. These were the various recommendations of the Massey commission.
The fields of natural history and human history are quite separate on a national basis. In the field of human history you have archaeology and ethnology, while in the field of natural history you are dealing with zoology and geology as well as some other sciences. The Massey commission was very firm in its recommendation that there should be two distinct museums as soon as possible, and that is what is being done now. The reason for doing so is that, as our country grows, we should be in a better posi-
157$	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources tion to give to the people of Canada a better knowledge of natural and human history in order that they will make better citizens.
One can find examples of this division of museums in the various countries of the world. For instance in France you have the Musee de l'Homme, which is the French name for the museum of human history. In any country which is any kind of a country you will find both types of museums. For instance, in the city of London there are two British museums, one dealing with natural history and the other one with human history.

speechtext:
I think there is going to be duplication. As the minister says, there is a museum in Toronto, and I know there is one in the city of Saint John which gives the history of the peoples of the maritime provinces for the last 300 or 400 years. It deals also with natural history. I do not see why a young country like Canada should feel there is a necessity for two museums in Ottawa, as well as a museum in practically every province in the country. If there is


money to be spent on museums, then I feel that some of these museums in places like New Brunswick which are having difficulty with finances should be given financial assistance. Otherwise, there is bound to be duplication.
We are going to have the history of the maritime provinces represented in certain museums in the east; we are going to have the history of Ontario in the Toronto museum, and in Quebec, the history of Quebec. The same thing would occur right across Canada, so why should we duplicate that work in Ottawa with two museums? Frankly, I do not see the need for two distinct museums. We have a splendid museum established here now and I think we should develop it along the lines upon which it has been developed. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
I was glad to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland, Mr. Chairman, when he was speaking about some of the methods by which human history is recorded. We have in our province, and it happens to be in my city, a unique experiment in that type of thing. Man's history, of course, has been written in books, written on stone and by various other methods, but I think this one is perhaps unique.
I was interested, too, in the statement by the minister that, so far as he and his department are concerned, they would be pleased to give assistance to various types of museums throughout the country. It is on that statement that I base my hope the particular museum in which I am interested will receive some assistance.
I think perhaps the history of western Canada from the period of 1890 onwards has been largely neglected by historians. I am thinking of the geographical area when I refer to western Canada, and it has been neglected from the point of view of writings. I suppose it is because the people were pioneers and they had to concern themselves with other things, so they did not have time to write their history in books even though they were writing it without knowing it by another method.
There have been one or two books written. I might refer, for example, to the biography of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, as one of the books that has been written which throws some light on the period. I have criticized that biography, not because the Minister of Agriculture is not a picturesque character and typical of that part of history, but because I do not think it is much of a job, as a book. The last time I suggested that, the minister said I might

write a better one myself. I pleaded guilty to the ability, but not to having the time.
Now, to come to the meat of my subject; the thing to which I referred is a museum called the "Pion-Era" museum in the city of Saskatoon. The Minister of Agriculture, who I see is in his seat, knows as much about it or perhaps more than I do. It is unique. It is the history of Saskatchewan for the last 70 or 80 years written in the agricultural implements of the country. I visited it and I was amazed at the educational value of that project. I was amazed at the different attitude or the different way in which people approached that project. It was different from their approach to the ordinary exhibition with its midways and ballyhoo. I saw family after family, wives and children, who were there for the particular reason of educating themselves in the recent and not so recent past of their province. This project started as a very small museum to which people were invited to bring or send old buggies, old threshing machines, old red river carts. There is even an ancient hearse there which reminds us that man after all is mortal, but it is the implements that draw the attention.
You can read the history, step by step, of those earlier pioneers of Saskatchewan from the days when they came west from Ontario, bringing with them things like treadmills for the purpose of threshing grain, treadmills by which water was lifted from wells by the action of a dog running around a wheel, and so on. You can see what has been done by the efforts of a number of men, and I pay tribute to Mr. J. L. Phelps and to the curator, Mr. Shepherd, who has been invaluable in that organization.
They have built up a tremendous thing there. It is sitting on a piece of land which is the property of the organization. I think it is 70 acres in extent. They have a very large covered building which protects those implements. They have a staff of workers, carpenters and the like, who repair those ancient implements that are sent in. There you can see the various means of seeding, the various means of threshing, the development of modern farming all up through the years. That is the museum itself.
In recent years the people there, and 1 think rightly so, have expanded it into an exhibition of sorts. It is not at all for the purpose of making money; it is merely so those old pioneers may come there and bring their children and their grandchildren and show them the conditions under which the pioneers lived and the implements with which they worked in those early days.
They have reconstructed to some extent the life of the prairie homesteader, and for four or five days one can see those activities not 82715-100
Northern Affairs and National Resources simply in imaginary form but in actual fact. Perhaps the minister has attended on one of those days. I have no doubt he has and he would have seen, as I have, oxen-particularly trained for the purpose, because we now have no oxen in Saskatchewan-hauling the plows as in those former days. It brought me back to my own homestead days of four-on teams hooked up to a 14-inch breaking plow, and those big Reeves steam engines hauling 12 or 14 plough bottoms just as they were on the prairies in those days.
My plea is that this sort of thing should have some support. That sort of thing is the book which has not been written but which is in the process of being written, except that instead of pages and words, there are being used the implements showing the actual conditions under which people worked. A part of this particular show consisted of a sod house. You had the people there, the ladies dressed in the costumes of away back in the 1890's, carrying on their daily work.
As to the financial end of the project, it has always been a marvel to me how it has been supported. I appealed to the minister three or four years ago. I told him about it. I hoped that if he were ever passing through my city he would call in and see it. I do not believe he did, but perhaps I am doing him an injustice. If he did not, I would urge him to consult the Minister of Agriculture, and if the Minister of Agriculture could persuade him to go, that would please me greatly.
Now, as to the financial side, this sort of thing costs a lot of money. It is true that they charge entry fees on these days every summer. They have turned it into a sort of second Saskatoon agricultural exhibition with, as I say, purely educational and historical features rather than the usual commercial sort of thing that we have come to think of in exhibitions. In spite of their care and good management they have been going behind financially on this show, and I would like to set forth its requirements. I hold in my hand a letter from the secretary which arrived providentially on this very day. I had no idea that they were now organizing the matter, but they find themselves short of money and they think that they can qualify for both provincial and dominion grants.
This letter was written to me by Mr. Le-Beau, who has no idea that I am going to use it or that I might raise the question. I think it is a circular letter that has been sent to many friends of the organization. It states that the committee in charge are prepared to go ahead and stage their "Pion-Era" in 1957 if a reserve fund of $25,000 can be secured to underwrite it for this first year
1578	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources and to make some additional capital improvements. The letter goes on to say:
We have been assured that il 50 per cent of these funds can be raised in Saskatoon and surrounding districts, that the provincial and federal governments will make matching grants and thereafter an annual grant to continue "Pion-Era" as an annual event.
According to this letter it would seem that the condition for such assistance from the two governments mentioned would be the raising of a considerable sum of money on the part of private citizens themselves, and I fancy it was in that connection that the secretary wrote to me in the hope that I would be prepared to give a subscription to that particular fund. But I do urge upon the government and the minister the necessity of looking into this thing to see if it is not a tremendously worth-while project, in that it is the picture of human history so far as Saskatchewan is concerned.
After all, Saskatchewan until now has always been primarily an agricultural province, and the history of Saskatchewan therefore must need be the history of an agricultural people. Until the time comes when some author will blossom out and write a substantial and dependable work upon that province and its pioneers I think this museum and yearly exhibition provide the very best history of the province that we have.
This particular exhibition, if one can call it that, is becoming internationally known, certainly in some fields and in some directions. I should put the name of the organization on record. It is the western development museum in Saskatoon. John Fisher, executive secretary of the Canadian Tourist Association, said on his recent visit to Saskatchewan that some day the exhibition may well rival the famed Calgary stampede as a tourist attraction, and I heartily agree. Quite frankly, I am not so interested in whether or not it becomes a tourist attraction. What I am interested in is that this history of my province may be made permanent through some well-deserved public assistance.
I could go on, but I think I have made my point. I would urge the minister to give it some consideration.

Mr. Chairman, while we are discussing this resolution and museums in general I should like to take this opportunity to say that in the constituency which I represent, Cape Breton North and Victoria, there was opened last summer a museum which I might say, with all deference to my hon. friend from New Brunswick, cannot be duplicated. It was erected in recognition of


a great humanitarian, one of the greatest men of all ages. I refer to Dr. Alexander Graham Bell.
It is perhaps fitting that this museum has been erected on the grounds or near where Dr. Bell did most of his experimenting and very much of his research work, particularly in the field of aviation.
It was at Baddeck that he experimented with and produced the first heavier than air machine to fly in the British Empire. I might say, too, sir, that it was Baddeck this great man chose as his last resting place. He and Mrs. Bell are buried at Beinn Breagh surrounded by the beautiful Bras d'Or lakes and by the brooding beauty of the Cape Breton hills.
This building is of unique design. When Dr. Bell experimented with his flying machines he built kites in a tetrahedroid shape, and this motif can be plainly discerned in the design of the building. I should like at this time to pay tribute to the great personal interest the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has taken in this building. He followed its development from the beginning with keen interest as did his predecessor in office, who is now the Minister of Public Works. We in Cape Breton North and Victoria and in fact all the people of Nova Scotia are greatly indebted to the minister and his staff for the great interest they displayed and their efforts on our behalf in order that we might have this great museum.
I should also like to pay tribute to the family of Dr. Alexander Graham Bell, the Grosvenor family and the Fairchild family. Mrs. Fairchild and Mrs. Grosvenor are daughters of Dr. Bell. At considerable expense and sacrifice they gathered together all the things of interest that touched on the life of Dr. Alexander Graham Bell. At this time I should also like to pay tribute to the staff of the museum, who are always so interested in this great collection and who are consistently courteous to the tourists who visit the museum by the thousands during the summer.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a number of interesting speeches requesting the establishment of museums in various parts of Canada or financial assistance for those already established, and a considerable amount of historical fact or fancy has been introduced simultaneously, all of which while it has been interesting perhaps has had very little to do with the resolution actually under discussion, which proposes to divide the national museum into two separate museums.
The minister seems to think he scored a great victory over me in connection with the British museum. I said the British

Northern Affairs and National Resources
museum was under one administrative head, and as a matter of fact the British museum is in that position. I think the remarks of the minister served only to indicate that he has finally discovered that there is more than one museum in the United Kingdom, a fact with which most of the rest of us were already acquainted. As I say, the British museum is still under one head; there are of course numerous museums in the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS

speechtext:
However, the British
museum is perhaps the world's greatest, and this extremely large institution is under one administrative head and it has various branches, departments and sub-departments. As a matter of fact the branch dealing with archeology and the ancient civilizations of the Greeks, Egyptians and Phoenicians has more exhibits than are contained in the whole Canadian national museum. Nevertheless they do not find it necessary to establish a separate museum with a separate administrative set-up for each department. As a matter of fact what the minister is proposing in this resolution, as far as I can see, is tantamount to proposing to divide the Department of Agriculture into two separate departments, one to deal with livestock and the other to deal with plants and crops; the ideas are similar.
I think all of us are anxious to increase the exhibits on display in our national museum and to generally improve it, but in my opinion this will not be best accomplished by what the minister is proposing in this resolution. As a matter of fact I think it is extremely likely that what he is proposing here will have exactly the opposite effect, and we will have a poorer museum than would be the case if we devoted our time and effort to establishing one good museum under one head.
The minister said the cost involved in the new administrative set-up would be comparatively small, but he indicated there will be one new director employed at a salary of $10,000 a year and four other people including an administrative officer, two other employees and a typist or something of that nature. The total cost of the new staff for salaries alone would be not less than $25,000, I would estimate, including $10,000 for the director and $15,000 for the balance of the staff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS

speechtext:
Yes. The total amount to be voted this year for the museum is $328,000. This new administrative set-up is going to constitute 7 or 8 per cent or possibly 82715-100J
more of the total amount of money we are expending on museums. I maintain that this; money could be put into archeological research, and should be devoted to increasing the number of exhibits in our museums and things of that sort rather than in effect being wasted by establishing a new administration for the divided national museum. Our national museum is not going to be so large for many years to come that it cannot function efficiently under one head and with one administrative staff. The increase in staff ia to a large extent a waste of money which could be used to build up the museum, to increase the exhibits and improve things generally. It is nothing more than the setting up of some unneeded jobs.
From what the minister has said already in answer to one or two other questions I take it that the action being provided for in1-this resolution has already been taken, that the museum has already been divided in two, that two directors have been appointed and that administrative staffs have been taken on. In other words the action we are now presumed to be taking in this chamber has already taken place; it is a fait accompli.
I should like to ask the minister under what authority this has been done and these appointments made. The estimates passed last year provided for a salary of $8,600 for the chief curator, who was the head of the museum. This man has now been made one of the directors. The supplementary estimates provided for one full-time position at $9,850. I presume that item was put in the supplementary estimates to provide for the new director the minister is now talking about. I did not understand that position was being provided for when the supplementary estimates were dealt with last summer.
My questions still stand. What authority is there for the division of the museum in two, which has taken place? Under what authority were these extra administrative people taken on, these people who apparently have been working for several months?

This was done in accordance with the power given the minister under the act. I do not agree with the hon. member when he says the number of administrative jobs has been doubled. The two new directors are not acting only as administrative officers. These men are scientists and research men of great reputation, and each will be able to do a great deal of research work in his own respective field. We were most fortunate to obtain their
1580	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources services as research men and as men of science, not especially as directors. They are there to do research work.

speechtext:
Dr. Russell is a master of arts and a Ph.D. in paleontology which degrees he obtained from Princeton University. He was in Ottawa from 1930 to 1937, and has been with the national museum since 1950. Prior to that date he held several important appointments with the University of Toronto and the Royal Ontario Museum. During the war Dr. Russell was commissioned as a captain and saw service overseas. He served in several staff positions until November, 1945, when he was demobilized with the rank of major.
The outstanding contributions of the new director of the natural history branch of the museum are in the fields of vertebrate paleontology, particularly that of western Canada. He has also made several contributions to the fields of invertebrate paleontology, geology, zoology and museology. Since 1950 Dr. Russell has served as secretary treasurer of the Canadian Museum Association.
Dr. Jacques Rousseau received his early schooling in Quebec and obtained his B.A. in 1926 from the University of Montreal. He obtained an L.Sc. in 1928 and a D.Sc. in 1934 from the same university. Dr. Rousseau's teaching career began at the University of


Montreal in 1935. In 1938 he became assistant director of the Montreal botanical gardens, and its director in 1944. It was during this period that the Montreal botanical gardens were created and achieved wide renown across Canada.
Dr. Rousseau, for 30 years a professional botanist of distinction, has devoted much time to ethnology since 1932. He has studied especially Algonkian ethnology and devoted some time also to Arctic pedology. Dr. Rousseau is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and of the Arctic Institute of North America. For many years he was a director and secretary general of the French Canadian Association for the Advancement of Sciences. Dr. Rousseau is on the editorial committee of Archives de Folklore and is a member of the American Anthropological Association as well as being a director of the Canadian Museum Association.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 157, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not so often that one has a bill which can have only one principle in it, but it so happens that this is one of that type. There is only one objective in the bill, and that is to increase the payments in connection with prairie farm assistance; and that objective runs all through its terms.

There are five categories under which payments can be made under the act. The first is one which has not been operative since wheat went beyond 80 cents a bushel. The others-(b), (c), (d), (e)-have all been increased under this bill. The first item has to do with areas where the crop of wheat is more than five bushels and not more than eight bushels per acre. That is the top category in which payments have been made in recent years.
In dealing with that I should point out that payments are not made on wheat. A great deal of the discussion that goes on in connection with this bill would suggest that the payments are made on wheat. That is not the case at all. Wheat is only used as a barometer to indicate how dry it is in a district, arid for no other reason. Hence if it was only dry enough to put the crop down to more than five bushels and not more than eight bushels, then that is the category in which the lowest payments are made.

Then in (c), if the yield is
more than three bushels and not more than five bushels per acre, the award shall be $3 per acre. There is an increase in both these. In the top one it is 50 cents and in the bottom one there is a new division in the areas. Therefore one cannot say that it is just 50 cents. It is $1.50 above the lowest payment that was made there previously and 50 cents above the highest payment. Then we come to the third which is with regard to crop failure, where there is a crop which is so low, generally speaking, that there is nothing to deliver to the elevator. Of course the item just referred to by my hon. friend, flooded area, is in the same classification. That is where water has been on the land and therefore there is not any crop.
When the question is asked as to what the differences are in payments now as compared with payments in 1939, those are the main facts that must be considered. A man does not need to have anything at all but livestock, arid he can still draw. He does not require to have anything but hay lands, and he can still draw. He could have all his lands summer fallowed in a particular year and still draw. In other words he may farm his land as he thinks
Prairie Farm Assistance Act it ought to be farmed, and if it is dry in the area where he is farming he gets paid. It does not make any difference whether he has wheat or whether he has oats, barley, rye, flax or only pasture; he can get paid. The definition of "cultivated land" makes that very clear. Those who have had the feeling that this is only to take care of wheat growers are scarcely correct in any criticisms that are made along those lines.
The number of acres for which an award may be made has been amended, and that also results in increases. If a man has the limit of 200 acres and you multiply 200 by the figures I have just given, it would indicate that there will be an increase. The section that deals with the minimum has not been changed. Under the old act the minimum was $200 and it is still $200 in the amending bill. There had to be some changes in that section simply for the purpose of putting in the lettering to which this section referred.
Then when we come down to the last section we deal with the matter of blocks. I may say that one of the reasons for having straight lines in the first act was to avoid the very thing that brought about some criticism during the debate on the resolution. We were not attempting to deal with all the area that should be taken care of in a drought period, nor have we been taking care of all the area that should be taken care of because of flooding. It was assumed right from the beginning that the initial responsibility in all three western provinces was with the municipality. Then it was assumed that when the load became too heavy for the municipalities or any one municipality, the province had a responsibility. When it was found there were at least 25 municipalities in a province affected by crop failures of one kind or another, particularly drought and grasshoppers, the federal government assumed some responsibility. The objective then under this bill is to have provision made whereby the federal government would take care of its responsibilities.
As hon. members will recall, in the period that just preceded the passing of the first legislation there were as many as 300 municipalities affected by drought, grasshoppers and everything that goes along with drought. The area was pretty much a solid block centring in southern Saskatchewan and spreading into both Alberta and Manitoba. Along the northern side of the area in Saskatchewan there was an area about which there was some question as to whether it should be in or out. The same thing could be said of areas in the south as the drought moved farther north. Up through Manitoba on the east side and Alberta on the west side there

Proirie Farm Assistance Act were always areas about which there was a considerable discussion as to whether they were in or out.
What was decided was that we would take blocks composed, as the act first provided, of complete townships. Then we would leave any partial townships to be taken care of by the municipalities or the province. It was never intended that there should be areas of which no one would take care. It was assumed that if these conditions were repeated the province would take care of part of it and the small needs would be looked after by the municipalities. I am referring to such things as providing seed and other things which still remain largely for the municipalities.
We went along for some time on that basis. Then it was evident that nothing was going to be done by the municipalities or the provinces, so it was suggested some amend-mends ought to be made. The indications were that some people, who were certainly entitled to it, were not getting assistance. We therefore, made provision for adding certain sections, or taking out certain sections that were outside the solid block or just along the edge of the solid block. Again we stayed with the straight line.
The reason for staying with the straight line was, as I said a moment ago, to avoid putting ourselves in the administration of the act in a position where we could select any individual at all and either put him in or take him out. If these people were entitled to some assistance it was expected that the province would utilize about the amount of money it had utilized prior to our coming into this field in order to take care of them. If it were a specialized case, or the case of a few individuals, it was felt that probably the municipality would take care of them, as the municipality has authority to do in all the provinces.
After having had some experience with these straight lines, we yielded to pressure in connection with the matter and made it contiguous areas. This section of the bill as it now is reads:
Where a block of contiguous sections of land or any block of settlement or river lots within an eligible township having an area of not less than one-sixth of the township and a side that lies along the boundary of an ineligible area is determined by the board to have an average yield of more than 10 bushels of wheat per acre, such block of land shall be ineligible for award.
It has been said over and over that hail does not follow a straight line; drought does not follow a straight line; grasshoppers do not follow a straight line, so by this provision you can swing inside an area where there is a block of six sections or

more that have 10 bushels of wheat to the acre, and say that is not dry enough to bring it under this act so it goes out because it is alongside an area which is out.
Then, on the other side, there is the next paragraph, paragraph (b), which provides for taking in sections where the dry area runs out over the solid block. The main reason for staying with straight lines in all these cases was so that no government or board or minister or deputy minister or anyone else could be accused of putting an individual in or taking an individual out. If he was out and needed help, then there was someone else who was supposed to give that help. If he was in and should be out, there was some provision for taking him out by using straight lines.
Again the question was raised as to why a man was in who had 20 bushels to the acre. One has to understand farming in the west in order to understand that. He may have had, say, 20 acres of the best land he had, land that had been summer fallowed, land that had been given very special care, in wheat and all the rest of his crop might be on inferior land as compared with the land on which he grew wheat. He might have' had 20 bushels of wheat to the acre, not because it was not dry in the area but because that piece of land had been given special care.
I would say that ninety-nine times out of a hundred where that condition existed he would have a lot of other crops that were not good. He would not be dependent on wheat for his existence. He might happen to have livestock, and when a man is dependent on livestock for his livelihood and has a grass failure he is in a worse position than the man who has just had a failure in wheat. The man who has a failure in wheat is not as hard up as the man who has livestock on land where there is not sufficient grass and who has to buy feed. I just want to emphasize the fact that this bill was not drawn to deal with wheat, it dealt with drought and the conditions that follow drought and more recently took in flooding.
Then we make it the contiguous sections. As a matter of fact I personally am opposed to this amendment being made at all, and I would say that if there are enough members in the committee to put it back where it was, with rectangular blocks, I am all for it. It can be discussed in the committee when we get there, as to whether it should be in or out; but it does have the effect of perhaps increasing slightly the payments which are made in general over the whole area, and to that extent I say it is within the principle of the bill in that it does increase payments. But when you start a

group of men working over an area that is comparatively dry it goes without saying that there are going to be areas in there with land a little better than some of the other land where, by zig-zagging around, you can put a fellow out.
If the fellow happens to be a good Grit and he is put out, well, nobody criticizes that because it is a Liberal government that is kicking him out, they say. But if it works the other way and it happens to be a good Liberal who is put in, well, that is all wrong. And, vice versa, if you, to use the same terms, are dealing with a good C.C.F.'er, if there are any, and he is put out, well, that is the government acting against its opposition. If he is brought in, then perhaps Liberals say, well, that is something you should not have done at all, so one is up against troubles in connection with it all the way through.
I must say that if the provinces and the municipalities were looking after what we thought they were going to look after when we brought in this legislation we would not have under consideration departing from the rectangular blocks, but we are departing from the rectangular blocks in this amendment. It will be brought before the committee, as was suggested the other day; at least I assume the house will agree that the bill should go to the committee.
I do not think there is anything more I need to say at this time apart from that. It is entirely on the principle of the bill, and the principle is to increase the payments above what they have been under the act as it was and there really is not any other principle in the bill but that. There is nothing more that I should discuss on the second reading, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest to the house that it is my wish, and I hope it is the wish of the house, to have this bill referred to the agriculture committee as soon as it is given second reading and have full discussion there on all the points in which we may be interested.

Mr. Speaker, I am not surprised at the question that was raised by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. The suggestion he made really contains the answer,

because in western Canada it is almost impossible to find an area where there is flooded land where the yield will not be higher than is stated in the act. But that does not apply to that section at all, and that is the reason it does not apply. If it has rained sufficiently to flood the land so it will not grow a crop, then that land automatically comes in even if it is in the middle of one of the best crop areas in the country.
The reason it has to be at least six sections is to ensure that the applicant will not be some person who is farming in a slough when it happens not to rain, and at other times when it rains he cannot farm. He probably gets good returns in the years when it is dry and other people do not get anything. It can hardly be made to apply to just one small area and so it was made 3,840 acres, which is six sections. The reason six sections are stipulated is to avoid all the other matters that have been criticized, mainly the straight lines. It is possible for it to zigzag around all over the place, and it does not have to be alongside any township. There is no question of having an area contiguous to or alongside another township. In fact it can be located right in the middle of a township, or it can include the four corners of four townships. Indeed, it can be located anywhere.
The reason there must be some limit on it is that as everyone knows there are areas in western Canada that are littered with what we call sloughs. You would not call them sloughs in eastern Canada; they may be described here as ponds or something else; but in dry country no matter where it is located there is a greater tendency for water to run into low places and stay there when there is no outlet. The same condition obtains in the vicinity of the Dead sea and in other areas where there is great drought. The water keeps running into those low places, and one cannot farm there in wet years.
The act states that if you were able to farm in three years out of the previous five, then you can come in under the act; but if you were not able to farm for three years out of the previous five because of water the land would be considered a natural slough area and the position taken would be that you should not be paid for not being able to farm an area that had water on it more often than not. That is the general principle underlying the provision.
There is another matter in this connection, and of course we only learn about some of these things as we go along. The act states that there has to be a continuous area. Our general difficulty in connection with this has been that there are areas where there always have been many sloughs except in drought 82715-10X4
Prairie Farm Assistance Act years, when in all probability they dried up; but in all other years they contained water. There is some difficulty in determining how much of the slough had water in it all the time and how much around the outside came about only because of the flooding.
For example, I received a letter yesterday from a man, and it was the third time he wrote me. We sent inspectors out on two previous occasions to attempt to convince him that he was not right, but now he has a petition as long as your arm and he has sent it in to prove that he is right.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources for
1957-58 provide for substantially increased activities in northern Canada, for continuing major developments in the national parks, for expanded activities in the forestry field, for a continuation of important studies in the field of Canada's water resources, and for an important increase in the field of travel promotion.
For the department as a whole the estimates for 1957-58 total approximately $46,400,000, an increase of about $8,400,000 over the previous year. Almost three-quarters of this increase is devoted to northern development. Important projects include bridges in the Yukon, a major program on the construction of the highway to Yellowknife at a cost of over $2,500,000, the construction of two hostels and a 25-classroom school at the new site of Aklavik at a cost

of almost $2 million, the completion at a cost of $1 million of the hostel and school at Fort Smith and the commencement Of a hostel and vocational training school at Yellowknife at a cost of $1 million. Many other projects are of course provided for, including housing for Eskimos at various locations and improvements to educational facilities.
In the national parks and historic sites the over-all program has been held at about the same level, but adequate provision has been made for the continuation of the redevelopment of major park highways. This program includes some $3 million for further work on the Banff-Jasper highway in Alberta, some $3,100,000 for the Banff-Windermere highway in British Columbia, $1 million for the Cabot trail in Nova Scotia and $700,000 for the Gulf Shore road in Prince Edward Island. Major reconstruction at Halifax citadel will be continued, an important development at Signal Hill in Newfoundland will be undertaken, and restoration of Fort Langley, British Columbia will be completed.
In the water resources field the field studies program on the Columbia river has been reduced as work is nearing completion, but this has been counterbalanced by provision for expanded hydrometric survey work across Canada, by provision for increased expenditures on studies by the lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba board, and by provision of $100,000 for special studies required in the development of water use policy.
Major increases are requested in the appropriations of the forestry branch. These include an added $325,000 for contributions to the provinces under the Canada Forestry Act, this increase being made necessary by the provision of some $500,000 to assist the provinces for the first time in the field of forest fire protection. An increase of about $335,000 is provided to assist in the fight against the spruce budworm in New Brunswick, where it is now apparent that an expanded program is required in the coming year. The other major increase lies in the completion of the construction of the laboratory for the pulp and paper research institute of Canada near Montreal. This project was commenced in 1956-57 and should be completed in 1957-58, at a total cost of about $2,250,000.
The regular program of the Canadian government travel bureau will be continued, but provision is being requested in the 195758 estimates to cover a special campaign at a cost of about $300,000 to stimulate travel to Canada's Atlantic provinces, whose economies are dependent to a considerable extent on the tourist industry.
