The house in committee on Bill No. 16, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company and certain wholly owned subsidiaries -Mr. Mcllraith-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Short title.

Mr. Chairman, before this measure carries I have a few words to say, because the bill is of some importance to a good number of constituents whom I have the honour to represent. The explanatory note in the bill reads in part as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to simplify the corporate organization of Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
The remarks I intend to make and the amendments I intend to move are in an effort to simplify the life of some of my constituents. This somewhat routine, under ordinary circumstances, bill contains the names of two railway companies which have served a region that has a very interesting and particular history. I refer particularly to that part of British Columbia that lies between Nakusp on the Arrow lakes and Kaslo on the Kootenay lakes, and the two companies in question are the Kaslo and Slocan Railway Company and the Nakusp and Slocan Railway Company.
I said these railroads had served a country with a particular history, in the first instance a history of some dramatic incidents, first of all in the discovery of silver and other ores in the early 1890's. I am not going to expatiate on that aspect of the development, because I think other members possibly have a closer and more personal knowledge of that period. It is also a country in which there have been many famous men and, from what I hear, though not from personal experience, many famous women.
Private Bills
Then there was the very interesting and famous strike that occurred in the Slocan country, which was one of the most interesting incidents in the labour history of British Columbia. The strike was brought about by a contest between some very ruthless American capitalist owners of the mines in question in the Slocan country and the miners who were members of the western federation of miners. The strikers were quite peaceful and were simply asking for what would be considered today a very modest increase in wages and very slight improvements in their working conditions. But the then attorney general of the province became so excited over the situation that he gave orders for a regiment of British Columbia troops to be moved into the Slocan country to stop the strike.
Iam very glad to be able to say that it was the uncle of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, who was then a member of the provincial house, who saw the foolishness of this action and persuaded the premier of the province of the time to have the order cancelled. That was the late Senator Green, and it was largely for that reason that the late Senator Green, while he was the member for Kootenay West, could run as a Conservative and get a majority of the labour votes in the constituency.
This region was also the scene of the first great organization of the western federation of miners in southeastern British Columbia They came over from the United States and an organization was required, and the core ot that organization was in the then city of Sandon and the present city of Kaslo. There were many very interesting incidents surrounding the early organization of the federation.
Then there was a period of extremely rapid growth when Kaslo as a matter of fact, was the capital of the Kootenays, a period that saw a phenomenal building of railroads, building of roads, discovery of mines, and so on. Shortly after that came a period of very rapid growth and great production of ores throughout that region.
In addition, the region these two railroads serve has been a country of several important firsts. That is a very common thing in the constituency I happen to represent. There was the first organization of the western federation of miners, the first drafting of a socialist program in British Columbia in the then city of Sandon in 1885, and the publication of the first socialist newspaper in British Columbia by Mr. Pettipiece, the paper being the Lardeau Eagle. Then there was the first development-I think the Minister of Fisheries will know something about this because while he is an expert on fisheries

Private Bills
his early history is more connected with the development of the mining industry-of certain processes for the milling of ores in the Slocan country. This involved the development of successful processes for the milling of certain ores which up to that date had been considered quite complex.
Then we have these two railroads, the terminal at one end being the village of Nakusp and at the other end the city of Kaslo. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was born in the city of Kaslo, and I am quite sure that before the debate is over we shall hear from him in connection with the bill. 1 was reborn in the village of Nakusp, and I may say that Nakusp is the most beautiful village in British Columbia and Kaslo and New Denver vie for second place as the most beautiful locations in the rest of the province.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is quite a bill.

Since 1890 there has been great production of ore in the Slocan portion of the area served by these railroads. There have been ups and downs largely occasioned by the fluctuating price of silver in the early days but tremendous wealth has been taken out of the Slocan country since 1890 up to the present time. Even since the war the production has been tremendous, though owing to the drop in the prices of silver and zinc production has been less in the last two or three years.
The mountains are full of ore. There are masses of ore in the country, and all that is necessary is satisfactory prices to enable the ore to be worked. Some mines are working very successfully at the present time, particularly Violamac close to Sandon. Since 1895 there has been increasing production of lumber, particularly in the Arrow lakes area but to some extent in the Slocan area and to a considerable extent around the Kaslo area. In addition both Kaslo and Nakusp are noted throughout Canada for their cherries and other fruit products.
The operation of these railroads was based on the necessity to haul the products of the mines and the woods to market, and they play a very important part in the economy of the district. I have just remembered that I was on a committee that welcomed the arrival of the first train from Kaslo to Nakusp, and if my memory serves me correctly the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was a passenger on that train.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: What year was that?

That was in 1914. That was the completion of the road. As a matter of fact the life history of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and my own have been

somewhat parallel, though unfortunately he has gone in the wrong direction in some things.
There has been some deviation lately.

As I said before, there has been millions of dollars worth of production from the mines in the area and from the woods and as far as the forestry industry is concerned there are possibilities for that production to be continued forever under proper forest management which I trust the present government of British Columbia will carry out. As far as the mining industry is concerned, I have talked to prominent mining engineers in the district, to members of the eastern British Columbia chamber of mines in Nelson, and I have read reports on the various mines published by Mr. Walker, deputy minister of mines in the province of British Columbia. There is no question about it, there are tremendous reserves of ore in that area.
Everything went along fairly well, with no one in the district anticipating any difficulties with respect to railroad transportation, until 1955. In June of that year we had a most unusual and severe storm in the district.
I should say that our country is very free of strong winds, storms and exceptional weather conditions. This quite unusual storm created a great many unusual freshets that washed out a good many sections of the Kaslo and Slocan railway between Parapet and Kaslo and I understand resulted in damage to the railroad amounting to something over $200,000. Shortly after that rumours began to go around the district to the effect that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was going to make application to the board of transport commissioners for the right to abandon the road between Kaslo and Parapet and between that portion of the line and Sandon, a total mileage in all of 35 miles.
The first I heard of it was in a letter I received from the Kaslo board of trade shortly after my return home following the session of that year. I will read the letter because it indicates the concern of the people there. I might say that the president of the board of trade in Kaslo was then the manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce there. He was a community-minded citizen who was greatly disturbed over the possibility of this line being abandoned. He had full knowledge of the situation, being the bank manager in the city of Kaslo. This is a copy of the letter which he wrote to the secretary of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and which is dated August 18, 1955. It reads as follows:

Dear Sir: Canadian Pacific Railway Company
re Kaslo to New Denver, B.C. Line As a result of a severe storm near the end of June last the above line was damaged to the extent that there has been no scheduled traffic over it since and no freight service over it of any kind.
It is now rumoured that the C.P.R. are applying through yourselves for abandonment of this line. Inquiries as to the truth of this move have been made by us direct to the C.P.R. but to date they have not given us any definite reply; however equipment is being moved out and all section maintenance crews are being laid off.
As you are probably aware this line runs in its entire distance through a very heavily mineralized area and since the 1890's there have been vast quantities of lead and zinc mined here. The recession in the past two years in base metal prices has brought these operations to a low point but as all who are familiar with mining know well this condition can change practically overnight, and in the over-all picture the railway has moved a large tonnage, all of it very vital to the economy of this area. In this area also are considerable stands of timber and poles.
This board and the people of this community are very disturbed at the prospect of the abandonment of this line and we intend to protest the move vigorously and to take the matter up through our federal representative in parliament-
In whom they have great confidence.
Oh, oh.

The letter continues:
-and through our members in the provincial government.
That letter, Mr. Chairman, was an official indication of the concern of the people of that area. In any event, the C.P.R. finally made application to the board of transport commissioners to abandon this 35 miles of right of way comprising the whole of that of the Kaslo and Slocan railway and a portion of that of the Nakusp and Slocan railway. That started things humming. There were meetings in Kaslo, Nakusp, New Denver and in Nelson which I attended. I did what I could to assist them in gathering information or by telling them where they could obtain it.
The matter was of such great importance to the mining operators in the Slocan and Kaslo country and to the lumber operators in that area that there was a particularly well co-ordinated effort put forth. There was co-ordination in the gathering of facts. There was co-ordination in the submission of evidence. There was unanimity and united opposition to this unexpected and unwarranted move on the part of the C.P.R.
As I said before, I attended these meetings and had the opportunity to witness the concern not only of the companies operating in the district but of the unions representing the workers in the district and of the people in the communities generally, and also the determination to do all they could to stop this application from being successful. Everything possible was done to get the
Private Bills
history of the whole situation. Incidentally I might mention at this time that these railroads were not only chartered under federal charter but were chartered under legislation in British Columbia. In one of those documents is a reference to the fact that, in return for certain subsidies, the C.P.R. agreed to keep the Kaslo and Slocan railway in operation forever. Apparently that reference was overlooked entirely.
In any event, all this effort on the part of the people concerned was to no avail and finally the application of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was granted by the board of transport commissioners. Unfortunately, owing to the C.P.R. strike which necessitated my taking devious modes and methods of transportation, although I arrived here on time I was unable to bring my trunks and other things. I could simply carry a briefcase and a suitcase. As a result I have not with me the file on this question. Since I arrived here the Arrow lakes have frozen up, there is no transportation to my ranch and I cannot get it. Hence I am largely obliged to rely on tidbits from here and there.
Anyway, I have in my hand a copy of the Kootenaian published in Kaslo, British Columbia, of January 24. It contains a headline "Abandonment Allowed", "Commission Grants C.P.R. Request to Abandon Kaslo-Denver Line". It am just going to quote the article because it quotes from or publishes the judgment. The article reads as follows:
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been granted leave to abandon its line between Kaslo and New Denver.
In a letter received here by W. J. D. Walker, chairman of the abandonment committee of district organizations opposing the abandonment at a board of transport commission hearing at Nelson a year ago, chief commissioner Mr. Justice John D. Kearney has stated:
"1. Abandonment of operation of the Sandon branch between Parapet and Sandon is approved.
"2. Abandonment of the railway between Kaslo and Denver Canyon, other than the Sandon branch is approved, subject to the condition that as soon as said operation is abandoned, the C.P.R. shall reconvey to the crown in the right of the province of British Columbia all its rights, title and interest in and to the railway right of way of the line between Kaslo and Parapet.
"3. Neither the abandonment of operation approved in No. 1 or the conditional abandonment of operation approved in No. 2-
I want you to note that phrase "conditional abandonment".
-shall take place earlier than February 1, 1957."
The C.P.R. applied for leave to abandon the 33-mile line between Kaslo and New Denver and a two-mile branch line to Sandon after the June 1955 floods extensively damaged it. Company spokesmen at the hearing stated the C.P.R. had been losing money on the line in recent years-

Private Bills
Only in recent years. They made a great deal of money in previous years.
-as much as $49,838 in six months in 1955. That, coupled with the estimated $200,000 to repair it, made abandonment desirable, the C.P.R. felt. Counsel tor the C.P.R. was F. H. Britton of Vancouver, company solicitor.
Groups opposing the abandonment argued the present economy and future development of the area was largely dependent on the rail line. It was the area's only rail link and its abandonment would seriously affect the economy of the entire Slocan.
Opposing the abandonment were Cody-Reco Mines Limited, represented by J. R. Reyeroft; the B.C. attorney general's department, boards of trade and chambers of commerce of Kaslo, Slocan district and Nakusp, city of Kaslo and villages of New Denver and Silverton, whose counsel was L. S. Gansner of Nelson.
Mr. Justice Kearney, in his letter to Mr. Walker, stated the orders listed above were made "upon consideration of submissions on file and for reasons which will be given in a written judgment at a later date".
This means that the decision has been made. The only service or means of transportation between Kaslo and New Denver at the present time is a very narrow road, more properly termed a goat trail. Over this very narrow road thousands of tons of ore have to be trucked at the present time, and there is likely to be a great deal more in the future. With these vast quantities of ore to be moved, and without any doubt the development of highway and other traffic in the future between Kaslo and New Denver as well as other parts of the interior, it is essential that the present railway right of way be converted into a highway. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will agree, knowing the geography as well as I do, that the present railway right of way provides the only route for the development of a satisfactory highway between Kaslo and New Denver. In the early days the railways always got the choice sites in the bottom of the valleys. The roads built since that time have had to be built higher up at considerable expense to the public in many cases, as is witnessed along the Fraser canyon.
We were informed in the committee that the Canadian Pacific has taken some steps to implement the part of the board of transport commissioners' decision which mentions that the road had to be offered to the government of British Columbia. The Canadian Pacific has offered the right of way to the government of British Columbia, I understand, but to date there has been no response to that offer. I would not for a moment question that in the strict legal sense, according to the terms of this bill, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company takes over the responsibilities and obligations of the Kaslo and Slocan railway and the Nakusp and Slocan
[Mr. Herridge.l
railway. But this is a very important matter to the people living between New Denver and Kaslo. It is a very important matter to those people whose living depends on the continued development of that district. While in the strict legal sense one could say that these names could be included in this bill because the Canadian Pacific, by incorporating these companies into the main system, assumes the responsibilities and obligations of those companies, I feel there is a certain psychological advantage that can be gained for the people I have the honour to represent, and I hope later on a material advantage, by having the names of the Kaslo and Slocan railway and the Nakusp and Slocan railway deleted from this bill.
I am sure this will not cause a great deal of inconvenience to the Canadian Pacific. Next year the company intends to come before the committee and ask that certain other subsidiary companies be washed out and incorporated in their main system. I feel, in view of the fact that this highway is so important to the people of the area, that the deletion of these names from this bill, and holding over final transfer of these companies to the main company, will emphasize the importance of this matter to the people I have the honour to represent, and emphasize to the company and the government of British Columbia their desire for the consummation of the order of the board of transport commissioners.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, at a later stage in this debate I intend to move certain amendments with a view to having the names of these two companies removed from this bill not in any spirit of criticism of the Canadian Pacific but simply because I consider -withholding approval might be a spur to action by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do all it can to see that this order is completed, and a spur to the government of British Columbia to accept this right of way and build the necessary highway for the people residing between Kaslo and New Denver.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a few words to the remarks just made by my old comrade and good friend the hon. member for Kootenay West. The request he has made, of course, affects the people in his own riding very seriously. In view of my own old association with that district, which continues up to the present time, I too am very much concerned that everything that can be done will be done to help the residents of that district.
Last year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company started on a course of absorbing 37 subsidiary companies. Last session they dealt

with 13 of those companies and the bill was brought before this house in the usual way, then referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. It was duly adopted. This year the company has brought in a bill covering 12 more subsidiaries. When this bill was in the other place the sponsor explained that in 1958 a bill would be introduced covering the remaining 12 companies. What the hon. member for Kootenay West and I are asking is to have these two companies, the Kaslo and Slocan railway company and the Nakusp and Slocan railway company, deleted from the bill and left over to be dealt with in the bill which is being brought in next year.
We make that suggestion because, as he has very ably pointed out, there is unfinished business in so far as these two particular subsidiary companies are concerned. An order was made by the board of transport commissioners, I think less than a month ago, giving leave to abandon the line owned by the Kaslo and Slocan railway company and also a few miles of the line owned by the Nakusp and Slocan railway company. There was a condition attached to that order, namely that the railway company must convey the right of way on which the line was being abandoned to the provincial government. There has not yet been time to have that condition carried out. What we are concerned with is that there shall be no delay in the carrying out of that condition. We believe it is much more likely to be carried out quickly if the two companies are taken out of the present bill.
The difficulty in the district started in 1955 when there were quite disastrous floods, particularly in the city of Sandon. In that province in the early days those small towns could be incorporated as cities, and although the city of Sandon has perhaps only a half dozen or a dozen residences it is still a city. Those floods washed out the track in that particular part of the constituency and did a lot of damage. There is no question of that. But I have always believed that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was rather quick on the trigger when it moved at once to get an order to abandon the line. I do not believe it needed to do that. The officials saw an opportunity to get out of that district, and they made the application. It was opposed by the communities affected, not only by their councils but also by their boards of trade and by the mining companies which have been carrying on mining operations in the district, and also by the provincial government.
During the hearings the question of how the area was to be served if the railway
Private Bills
was abandoned became very prominent. I hold in my hand a press dispatch of February 2, 1956, from the Vancouver Sun, headed:
C.P.R. Urged to Give Rail Line to Government
Transport commissioner advises deal for Kaslo-New Denver road
The dispatch is from the city of Nelson, which is also in my hon. friend's constituency. It reads:
The Canadian Pacific Railway should give the British Columbia government its Kaslo-New Denver branch line and $75,000, Mr. Justice John D. Kearney suggested here Wednesday.
The rail company should then ask the government to build a highway, he said.
He advanced his suggestion as the board of transport commissioners ended a two-day hearing into the company's application to abandon the rail line.
It may seem peculiar that the chairman of the board of transport commissioners would make a suggestion that the C.P.R. should pay $75,000 to the province, but there is a story behind that, too. This railway from Kaslo to Sandon was originally a narrow gauge Great Northern line. The Great Northern went in from Kaslo to the mines in Sandon. The C.P.R. went in from Nakusp. There was pretty tough competition. I believe at one time one of the railways moved the station of the other line in the middle of the night. Those were hectic times in the district and there was very bitter feeling. I can remember that the city of Kaslo was of necessity a Great Northern town, and as a result it did not get many favours from the C.P.R., although that company ran a boat to the town.
Well, eventually the Great Northern stopped running the railway and after many negotiations, in which the provincial government was very directly involved, and a great deal of worry on the part of the mine operators and all the residents in the district, an arrangement was made under which the British Columbia government took title to the Great Northern part of the line and sold it to the Canadian Pacific Railway for $25,000 in 1912. Then, in addition, they gave the C.P.R. $100,000 to convert it into a standard gauge line and connect it up with their own line from Nakusp into Sandon.
Therefore the chairman of the board of transport commissioners was referring to that particular time when he suggested that the Canadian Pacific should pay back the $75,000 to the provincial government, that being the difference between what the C.P.R. had paid for the line originally and what the government had then paid over to the railway company. Mr. Justice Kearney was quoted in the press dispatch as having said:
"If I were the C.P.R.," Mr. Justice Kearney said, "I would just reverse the agreement of 1912 and

Private Bills
tell the government 'I want you to build the road. If you do I'll give you back the $75,000 you gave me and the railroad as well'.
And if I were the provincial government I'd talk business", he said.
That was in February of 1956.
I should like to ask a question for information. Was that suggestion made by the railway to the government, or was it merely a suggestion?

This was a suggestion by the chairman of the board of transport commissioners at the hearing at which the C.P.R. was applying for leave to abandon the railway.
Apparently the C.P.R. took no steps after that hearing to arrange for the transfer of the right of way to the provincial government. They may have done it, but no evidence was given in the committee the other day that such had been the case. The final order was not made by the board of transport commissioners until about a month ago, and in that order there was the condition that the C.P.R. must convey the right of way to the provincial government, but there was no provision that they must also pay the provincial government the $75,000. It may be that Mr. Justice Kearney decided that he did not have the power to make any such provision.
Subsequent to the order, the C.P.R. wrote a letter earlier this month to the provincial government initiating the negotiations for the conveyance of the right of way to that government. We were told in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines that there had not yet been a reply. Obviously it will take a little time to work out the details of a conveyance by the company to the provincial government. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, the title to this right of way, I believe, stands in the name of the Kaslo and Slocan railway company in so far as most of the distance is concerned and, for the other few miles, in the name of the Nakusp and Slocan railway company, being two of the companies which will be wiped out if this bill becomes law.
I do suggest, Mr. Chairman, to the members of the committee and to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that no harm would come to the C.P.R. if those two companies were dropped from the present bill and included in the bill which will be brought in in 1958. If they follow that course then both the railway and the provincial government will be under considerable pressure to get this question settled and to bring about the construction of a proper highway to replace the railway.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has said that the road at the present time is a very inferior one. One part of it which has

since been changed I think was the most dangerous road in British Columbia.
Many people preferred to walk up rather than drive in a car.
That particular part was changed a few years ago, but this highway as it exists at the present time is not suitable for carrying on the business in the district. There is a lot of logging being done, and of course the main industry is mining. The fact that there is no railway and no proper highway means that mines are shut down which might otherwise be operating. The families in the district have the breadwinners out of work, and it is an extremely serious situation for the people affected. They are a long way from Ottawa and it is just about impossible to overemphasize the difficulties under which they are labouring. In view of the fact that they are in the position where they have no railway and no proper highway, and will have to wait until the C.P.R. makes a transfer to the provincial government and until the provincial government sees fit to build a road, the result may be that nothing will be done for some years, and that would be a great tragedy.
I feel sure that if our suggestion is accepted and these two railway lines are deleted from the bill the practical result will be that the right of way will be conveyed to the provincial government rather quickly, certainly much more quickly than it would be in the normal course of events. That being the case the responsibility will be with the provincial government, and this parliament will at least have done its part. If the provincial government does not move to put in a highway, no one here can be held responsible. The very least we can do, Mr. Chairman, is to remove these two lines from the bill, thereby showing that we feel that the order made by Mr. Justice Kearney should be carried out without any further delay.
I hope the sponsor of the bill will again place this suggestion before the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. From their attitude in the committee the other day I do not believe they would be heartbroken if these two companies were deleted. Naturally they would probably prefer to have the bill go through just as presented, but I do not think they will worry very much if the two companies are taken out and brought back next year. I do hope they will see fit to fall in with the suggestion that has been made.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a word concerning this bill. When it was brought before the committee the sponsor did not seem inclined to favour the deletion of these roads from the

bill. As I listened to the discussion in committee and the debate we have had today I have been wondering it the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra would serve the purpose they have in mind. Both hon. gentlemen indicated that they wished to hasten the time when construction of the highway would get under way, and I support them to the fullest extent in their desire. I think there should be no undue delay in the construction of the highway to accommodate these people. I might point out that at the present time the government of British Columbia is doing a marvellous job in the construction of highways wherever it is possible to build them. In view of the rapidity and aggressiveness with which British Columbia is dealing with these problems I would think the construction of this highway would certainly be under consideration.
I do not advance this argument to offset in any way the amendment which will be proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West, but it does run in my mind that if the two roads were deleted from the bill at this time the result would be to delay construction of the highway for another two or three years. If we withdraw this section from the bill the result will be that a delay will occur in the transferring of the title of the right of way to the provincial government, and it is doubtful whether this action would hasten the construction of a highway to accommodate these people.
Oh, no.

That would be the result of your amendment. I would like to ask the sponsor of the bill a question. Has the British Columbia government been in contact with the department or with the board of transport commissioners concerning the deletion of this section from the bill? We are in committee, and perhaps the hon. member could reply at this time. Has there been any communication between British Columbia and the board of transport commissioners with regard to deleting this section from the bill?

I would have no means of knowing that but I am quite unaware of any. You will recall that the order became operative as of February 1. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company wrote a letter to the provincial government under date of February 6 dealing with the actual turning over of the right of way. An acknowledgment has come in under date of February 14 stating that a further reply would be forthcoming. Presumably the further reply merely has to do with certain materials that are to be retained by the railway company.
Private Bills
There has been no objection raised by the British Columbia government?
Not as far as the C.P.R. is concerned. There would be no occasion to object, as a matter of fact. I do not see how they could object to it.

It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, there should not be too much haste in trying to put this bill through at the moment. Another two or three days' delay in passing this bill might give us time enough to receive some communication from the British Columbia government indicating their attitude in this respect. We should learn if the recommendation of Mr. Justice Kearney whereby the railway would return $75,000 to the government of British Columbia will have any effect in hastening the construction of the highway. My understanding is that the railway has not been in operation since 1952-

-when the bridges were washed out, and it does not seem to me the railway is going to reconstruct the bridges. It appears they are using that as one of the excuses for not carrying on the operation of the line. I suppose their attitude is that there would be no point, since they would be abandoned anyway and so they will not spend the money for the reconstruction of the bridges. I believe the committee would be well advised to let the bill stand at this stage for a day or so, until there can be some confirmation of the position of the British Columbia government and its relationship with the C.P.R. in the transfer of this title to the provincial government.
I do not think we should be too hasty and act before we are a little clearer as to what is going to happen. We would like to see the people in this area have some sort of outlet. While I am not too familiar with the particular area, from what the two previous speakers have indicated it is necessary to have some sort of communication between the different localities and some way of getting out of these places. I think it would be a good suggestion to just report progress on this until we have a little further information.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should deal with the remarks of the hon. gentlemen in the order in which they were made. I must say that I found the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West so interesting and delightful that I wondered how quickly we would have the experience of finding all members of the House of Commons wanting to visit the two beautiful towns

Private Bills
in his constituency. I was quite carried away with his description of the beauty of the area which I have no doubt was quite right.
The difficulty in the matter stems from the fact that the point raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has no relevancy to the bill before the committee. I have no doubt that the people in the area are greatly concerned about having a proper highway in the area, and I did not want to prevent their case being stated by raising a point of order. Now that it has been so very adequately stated by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I think I owe a duty to them to point out that what the bill does is to vest all the undertakings, rights and privileges and so on in the Canadian Pacific Bailway. The two railway companies under discussion are wholly-owned subsidiaries and the Canadian Pacific must assume all obligations.
Does the bill not also dissolve one of those companies?

As I said, the Canadian Pacific must assume all the obligations of the subsidiary companies, even if the subsidiary companies are dissolved by the act. The people in that area will have to deal with the person who has leased the railway, who owns all the stock of the wholly-owned subsidiary, and against whom this order was made. The hon. members omitted to point out that the order was made against the Canadian Pacific Railway. Incidentally that order is signed by Hon. John D. Kearney.
I presume the committee would wish to have the terms of the order rather than only a report in a newspaper made a year or so ago. The order is quite clear. It makes the abandonment of the operation of part of the railway line under discussion dependent upon the conveying of the right of way of a designated piece to the province of British Columbia.
Could we have the exact terms of the order?
I could read the exact language.
How is it that the board of transport commissioners can order the Canadian Pacific to transfer to the government of British Columbia a right of way which belongs to another railway company?

They can do it for two reasons. The first is that the Canadian Pacific leased the right of way from the subsidiary for a long term of years. The Canadian Pacific is the owner of all the capital stock of the subsidiary companies.

I can understand the board of transport commissioners allowing the Canadian Pacific to abandon the operation of the line but I cannot see how the terms of an order to transfer a right of way would relate to the Canadian Pacific rather than the owners of the railway.

Perhaps I can clarify that a bit. The order permits the abandonment of a portion of the railway conditional on the reconveying of the right of way. In other words if the right of way is not reconveyed then they cannot abandon the line.
Does that mean the railway will have to reconstruct these bridges?
Yes it would. Perhaps I could read the order into the record as it is fairly short.
Go ahead.
If I have agreement I would ask that the preamble be included in the record and then I will read the operational part.

It reads:
In the matter of the application of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as lessee exercising the franchises of the Nakusp and Slocan Railway Company and of the Kaslo and Slocan Railway Company, for an order granting it leave to abandon the operation of that portion of the line known as the Kaslo subdivision of Canadian Pacific Railway Company between Kaslo and Denver Canyon, including the Sandon branch between Parapet and Sandon, all in the province of British Columbia, as applied for in the application dated September 15, 1955:
Upon hearing the application at a sitting of the board at Nelson, British Columbia, on January 30th, 1956, in the presence of counsel for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for the attorney general of the province of British Columbia and Kaslo board of trade, Slocan district board of trade, Nakusp chamber of commerce, the city of Kaslo and the villages of New Denver and Silverton and for Cody Reco Mines Limited: and upon consideration of the submissions on file and for reasons which will be given in a written judgment at a later date-
It is hereby ordered as follows:
1. The abandonment of operation of the said Sandon branch between Parapet and Sandon is approved.
2. The abandonment of operation of the said railway line between Kaslo and Denver Canyon, other than the said Sandon branch, is approved, subject to the condition that as soon as the said operation is abandoned Canadian Pacific Railway Company shall reconvey to the crown, in the right of the province of British Columbia, all its right, title and interest in and to the railway right of way of the said line between Kaslo and Parapet.
3.	Neither the abandonment of operation approved in paragraph numbered 1 hereof nor the

conditional abandonment of operation approved in paragraph numbered 2 shall take place earlier than the 1st day of February 1957.
John D. Kearney,
Chief Commissioner,
The Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada.

ACCIDENT PREVENTION AND TREATMENT-* DEFICIENCY DISEASES

Question No. 177-Mr. MacKenzie:
1.	Is the Department of National Health and Welfare taking any action toward the prevention and treatment of accidents, especially among children, involving poisoning from household remedies and chemicals?
2.	Does the Department of National Health and Welfare provide any assistance to the general practitioner in meeting the problem of deficiency diseases such as scurvy and rickets?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1. Yes. The food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare has collected data on the chemical composition of thousands of types and brands of household chemicals sold in Canada, including the name of the article, the manufacturer's
name and address, the dangerous ingredients, information to assist in diagnosis, antidotes, and methods of treatment.
Information has been prepared in a convenient form for ready reference and distribution to hospitals and other appropriate medical centres in the provinces to assist in the prompt treatment of accidental poisoning.
A pamphlet has also been prepared by the department warning parents about careless storage or handling of medicines and giving precautions to be observed when administering them to children. The pamphlet points as well to many other household chemicals as sources of danger.
The food and drug directorate plans to collect additional information about the number of accidental poisonings in Canada with a view to further careful study of this problem.
2. Yes. The nutrition division of the Department of National Health and Welfare maintains for the purpose of its nutrition surveys a laboratory equipped to determine the levels of various nutrients in very small blood samples. Since such laboratories are rare in Canada, the facilities of the nutrition division laboratory have been made available to all physicians.
Frozen blood samples are shipped to Ottawa for analyses for specific nutrients. The original arrangements are made between the provincial laboratories and the Department of National Health and Welfare but in practice the samples are usually shipped directly by the doctor to the nutrition division laboratory.
This service, which is relatively new, is being used increasingly by doctors in different parts of Canada. During the past year over 150 blood samples were sent in for analyses.
